claims.section: Introduction
claims.label: External conditions alone cannot explain complex coadaptations
claims.claim: Complex adaptations and coadaptations between organisms, such as the woodpecker's feeding structures or the misseltoe's dependence on particular trees, birds and insects, cannot be accounted for by the direct effects of external conditions such as climate and food.
claims.quote: it is preposterous to attribute to mere external conditions, the structure, for instance, of the woodpecker, with its feet, tail, beak, and tongue, so admirably adapted to catch insects under the bark of trees.
claims.scope: adapted structures of animals and plants, especially those involving relations with other species
measurable_quantities: magnitude of phenotypic plasticity induced by environment versus heritable trait differences
degree of trait matching between interacting species
claims.candidate_data: Common-garden and reciprocal-transplant studies of plasticity versus heritable divergence; interaction-network data such as the Web of Life database.

claims.section: Introduction
claims.label: Overproduction plus slight profitable variation leads to natural selection
claims.claim: Because more individuals of each species are born than can survive, there is a recurring struggle for existence, so any individual that varies even slightly in a way profitable to itself has a better chance of surviving and thus of being naturally selected.
claims.quote: As many more individuals of each species are born than can possibly survive; and as, consequently, there is a frequently recurring struggle for existence, it follows that any being, if it vary however slightly in any manner profitable to itself, under the complex and sometimes varying conditions of life, will have a better chance of surviving, and thus be _naturally selected_.
claims.scope: all animals and plants
measurable_quantities: offspring produced versus offspring surviving to reproduce
association between heritable trait values and survival or reproductive success
claims.candidate_data: Life-table and demographic data (COMADRE, COMPADRE), long-term individual-based field studies of selection, and experimental-evolution datasets such as the LTEE.

claims.section: Introduction
claims.label: Natural selection causes extinction of less improved forms and divergence
claims.claim: Natural selection almost inevitably causes much extinction of less improved forms of life and produces divergence of character.
claims.quote: we shall then see how Natural Selection almost inevitably causes much Extinction of the less improved forms of life and induces what I have called Divergence of Character.
claims.scope: all organic beings over evolutionary time
measurable_quantities: extinction rates of lineages
morphological disparity among descendant lineages over time
claims.candidate_data: Fossil occurrence and extinction data (Paleobiology Database) and time-calibrated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) with trait data.

claims.section: Introduction
claims.label: Species are not immutable but descend from other, mostly extinct, species
claims.claim: Species are not independently created and immutable; species of the same genus are lineal descendants of some other, generally extinct, species, just as varieties of one species descend from that species.
claims.quote: I am fully convinced that species are not immutable; but that those belonging to what are called the same genera are lineal descendants of some other and generally extinct species, in the same manner as the acknowledged varieties of any one species are the descendants of that species.
claims.scope: all species of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic relatedness of congeneric species
presence of extinct ancestral or stem taxa in the fossil record
claims.candidate_data: Molecular phylogenies and divergence times (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree, GenBank) combined with fossil occurrences (Paleobiology Database).

claims.section: Introduction
claims.label: Natural selection is the main but not exclusive means of modification
claims.claim: Natural selection has been the main, but not the only, cause of the modification of species.
claims.quote: Furthermore, I am convinced that Natural Selection has been the main but not exclusive means of modification.
claims.scope: all organic beings
measurable_quantities: proportion of phenotypic or sequence divergence attributable to selection versus other processes
strength of selection on traits in wild populations
claims.candidate_data: Compilations of selection gradients in wild populations, genome-wide scans for selection in GenBank/SRA data, and experimental-evolution results such as the LTEE.

claims.section: Causes of Variability
claims.label: Domesticated forms vary more among individuals than wild species do
claims.claim: Individuals of the same variety of long-cultivated plants and domesticated animals generally differ much more from each other than individuals of any one species or variety in nature.
claims.quote: they generally differ much more from each other, than do the individuals of any one species or variety in a state of nature.
claims.scope: older cultivated plants and domesticated animals compared with wild species
measurable_quantities: within-breed or within-variety phenotypic variance
within-population phenotypic variance in wild relatives
claims.candidate_data: Morphometric and trait datasets for breeds and their wild progenitors (e.g. TRY plant trait database for crops and wild relatives) and genomic variation data in GenBank/SRA.

claims.section: Causes of Variability
claims.label: Greater domestic variability is caused by changed, less uniform conditions
claims.claim: The greater variability of domestic productions is due to their being raised under conditions of life less uniform than, and somewhat different from, those of their parent species in nature.
claims.quote: I think we are driven to conclude that this greater variability is simply due to our domestic productions having been raised under conditions of life not so uniform as, and somewhat different from, those to which the parent-species have been exposed under nature.
claims.scope: domesticated animals and cultivated plants
measurable_quantities: phenotypic variance of populations raised under novel versus ancestral conditions
heritable variance generated per generation under changed conditions
claims.candidate_data: Experimental-evolution and stress-induced variation studies (e.g. Dryad experimental-evolution datasets) and common-garden comparisons of crops and wild relatives.

claims.section: Causes of Variability
claims.label: Variability arises mainly from effects on reproductive elements before conception
claims.claim: The most frequent cause of variability is that the male and female reproductive elements have been affected by the conditions of life before conception, the reproductive system being more sensitive to changed conditions than any other part of the organisation.
claims.quote: But I am strongly inclined to suspect that the most frequent cause of variability may be attributed to the male and female reproductive elements having been affected prior to the act of conception.
claims.scope: animals and plants under domestication or confinement
measurable_quantities: offspring variance as a function of parental environmental exposure before conception
fertility under confinement or cultivation
claims.candidate_data: Parental-environment and germline mutation-rate studies with sequencing data in GenBank/SRA; zoo breeding records such as those in ZIMS (Species360).

claims.section: Effects of Habit
claims.label: Inherited effects of use and disuse modify domestic animals
claims.claim: Habitual use and disuse of parts produce inherited changes in domestic animals; for example, domestic ducks have lighter wing bones and heavier leg bones relative to the skeleton than wild ducks because they fly less and walk more.
claims.quote: I find in the domestic duck that the bones of the wing weigh less and the bones of the leg more, in proportion to the whole skeleton, than do the same bones in the wild-duck; and I presume that this change may be safely attributed to the domestic duck flying much less, and walking more, than its wild parent.
claims.scope: domesticated animals
measurable_quantities: relative wing and leg bone mass in domestic versus wild ducks
trait differences in offspring of exercised versus unexercised parents
claims.candidate_data: Museum osteological collections (e.g. records accessible via GBIF and VertNet) for the morphological pattern; transgenerational experiments for the claimed cause.

claims.section: Correlation of Growth
claims.label: Selecting one trait unconsciously modifies other correlated parts
claims.claim: Because of laws of correlation of growth, when man selects for and augments any peculiarity, he almost certainly also modifies other parts of the structure without intending to.
claims.quote: Hence, if man goes on selecting, and thus augmenting, any peculiarity, he will almost certainly unconsciously modify other parts of the structure, owing to the mysterious laws of the correlation of growth.
claims.scope: domesticated animals and cultivated plants under artificial selection
measurable_quantities: correlated responses of unselected traits in selection experiments
genetic correlations between traits
claims.candidate_data: Artificial-selection experiment datasets (e.g. the Illinois long-term maize selection experiment, mouse and Drosophila selection lines on Dryad) and AnimalQTLdb.

claims.section: Inheritance
claims.label: Inherited peculiarities appear in offspring at the age they appeared in parent
claims.claim: A peculiarity tends to appear in the offspring at the same period of life at which it first appeared in the parent, though sometimes earlier.
claims.quote: A much more important rule, which I think may be trusted, is that, at whatever period of life a peculiarity first appears, it tends to appear in the offspring at a corresponding age, though sometimes earlier.
claims.scope: domesticated animals and plants, extended to organisms generally
measurable_quantities: age of onset of heritable traits or diseases in parents and offspring
claims.candidate_data: Pedigree databases of age of onset for heritable conditions, e.g. OMIA (Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals) and OMIM.

claims.section: Character of Domestic Varieties
claims.label: Domestic races differ like congeneric species, but usually less
claims.claim: Apart from their lesser uniformity, their often monstrous development of one part, and their fertility when crossed, domestic races of a species differ from each other in the same manner as closely allied species of a genus in nature, though in most cases to a lesser degree.
claims.quote: domestic races of the same species differ from each other in the same manner as, only in most cases in a lesser degree than, do closely-allied species of the same genus in a state of nature.
claims.scope: domestic races compared with closely allied wild congeneric species
measurable_quantities: morphological distance between breeds of one species
morphological distance between congeneric wild species
claims.candidate_data: Morphometric datasets of breeds (e.g. dog and pigeon skull morphometrics on Dryad) compared with wild-species trait data from museum collections accessible via GBIF.

claims.section: Origin of Domestic Varieties from one or more Species
claims.label: Any wild species domesticated as long would vary as much as existing domestics
claims.claim: Domesticated species were not chosen for an unusual inherent tendency to vary; any comparable set of wild animals and plants, bred under domestication for as many generations, would on average vary as much as the parent species of existing domesticated productions have.
claims.quote: I cannot doubt that if other animals and plants, equal in number to our domesticated productions, and belonging to equally diverse classes and countries, were taken from a state of nature, and could be made to breed for an equal number of generations under domestication, they would vary on an average as largely as the parent species of our existing domesticated productions have varied.
claims.scope: wild animals and plants brought into domestication
measurable_quantities: standing genetic and phenotypic variation in domesticated progenitors versus non-domesticated relatives
rate of phenotypic diversification under captive breeding
claims.candidate_data: Long-term captive-domestication experiments (e.g. the Novosibirsk farm-fox experiment) and genomic diversity data for wild species in GenBank/SRA.

claims.section: Origin of Domestic Varieties from one or more Species
claims.label: Domestic dogs descend from several wild species
claims.claim: Domestic dogs have probably descended from several distinct wild species rather than from a single one.
claims.quote: from geographical and other considerations, I think it highly probable that our domestic dogs have descended from several wild species.
claims.scope: domestic dogs and wild Canidae
measurable_quantities: genomic ancestry proportions of dog breeds from wild canid species
phylogenetic placement of dogs among Canidae
claims.candidate_data: Modern and ancient canid genome sequences in GenBank/SRA and the European Nucleotide Archive.

claims.section: Domestic Pigeons, their Differences and Origin
claims.label: All domestic pigeon breeds descend from the rock-pigeon
claims.claim: All domestic pigeon breeds, however different, have descended from the rock-pigeon (Columba livia) and its geographical sub-species, not from several aboriginal wild stocks.
claims.quote: I can feel no doubt that all our domestic breeds have descended from the Columba livia with its geographical sub-species.
claims.scope: domestic pigeon breeds
measurable_quantities: genomic ancestry of pigeon breeds
phylogenetic relationships of breeds to wild Columba species
claims.candidate_data: Whole-genome resequencing data for pigeon breeds and wild Columba in GenBank/SRA.

claims.section: Principle of Selection anciently followed, its Effects
claims.label: Domestic breeds arise mainly by man's accumulation of successive variations
claims.claim: Domestic breeds were not produced suddenly in their present useful form; their key cause is man's accumulative selection, nature supplying successive variations and man adding them up in directions useful to him.
claims.quote: The key is man’s power of accumulative selection: nature gives successive variations; man adds them up in certain directions useful to him.
claims.scope: domesticated animals and cultivated plants
measurable_quantities: cumulative response to selection over generations
historical trait trajectories of breeds and cultivars
claims.candidate_data: Long-term artificial-selection experiments (e.g. the Illinois long-term maize selection experiment) and breed-history genomic data in GenBank/SRA.

claims.section: Principle of Selection anciently followed, its Effects
claims.label: Races differ most in the parts man selects
claims.claim: Continued selection of slight variations in one part valued by man, such as leaves, flowers or fruit, produces races that differ from each other chiefly in that part, while other parts differ only slightly.
claims.quote: as a general rule, I cannot doubt that the continued selection of slight variations, either in the leaves, the flowers, or the fruit, will produce races differing from each other chiefly in these characters.
claims.scope: cultivated plant varieties within a species
measurable_quantities: among-variety variance in the selected organ
among-variety variance in unselected organs
claims.candidate_data: Crop germplasm trait records (e.g. USDA GRIN-Global germplasm evaluation data) and TRY plant trait database.

claims.section: Methodical and Unconscious Selection
claims.label: Unconscious selection over centuries modifies any breed
claims.claim: Unconscious selection, in which people simply breed from their best animals without aiming to change the breed, would over centuries improve and modify any breed, as methodical breeders have done within their lifetimes.
claims.quote: Nevertheless I cannot doubt that this process, continued during centuries, would improve and modify any breed, in the same way as Bakewell, Collins, etc., by this very same process, only carried on more methodically, did greatly modify, even during their own lifetimes, the forms and qualities of their cattle.
claims.scope: domesticated animals and cultivated plants
measurable_quantities: change in breed traits over historical time
trait differences between historical and modern specimens of a breed
claims.candidate_data: Ancient-DNA and archaeozoological time series of domestic animals and crops, and historical breed-standard morphometrics.

claims.section: Unknown Origin of our Domestic Productions
claims.label: Slow accumulated change hides the wild parents of old cultivated plants
claims.claim: Because a large amount of change has been slowly and unconsciously accumulated in long-cultivated plants, in many cases their wild parent-stocks can no longer be recognised.
claims.quote: A large amount of change in our cultivated plants, thus slowly and unconsciously accumulated, explains, as I believe, the well-known fact, that in a vast number of cases we cannot recognise, and therefore do not know, the wild parent-stocks of the plants which have been longest cultivated in our flower and kitchen gardens.
claims.scope: long-cultivated garden and crop plants
measurable_quantities: morphological divergence of crops from wild progenitors
duration of cultivation
claims.candidate_data: Crop wild relative inventories and phylogenomic data on crop origins (GenBank/SRA, Crop Wild Relatives inventory of the Crop Trust), with archaeobotanical dates.

claims.section: Methodical and Unconscious Selection
claims.label: Domestic races differ greatly externally but little internally
claims.claim: Because man can select mainly on externally visible deviations, domestic races differ greatly in external characters and relatively slightly in internal parts or organs.
claims.quote: We can, I think, further understand the frequently abnormal character of our domestic races, and likewise their differences being so great in external characters and relatively so slight in internal parts or organs.
claims.scope: domestic races of animals
measurable_quantities: among-breed variance in external traits
among-breed variance in internal organ size and structure
claims.candidate_data: Breed morphometric and anatomical datasets (e.g. dog and chicken breed studies on Dryad) and AnimalQTLdb trait records.

claims.section: Circumstances favourable to Man’s power of Selection
claims.label: Keeping large numbers of individuals favours successful selection
claims.claim: Because useful variations appear only occasionally, keeping a large number of individuals greatly increases the chance of useful variations appearing and is of the highest importance to success in selection.
claims.quote: But as variations manifestly useful or pleasing to man appear only occasionally, the chance of their appearance will be much increased by a large number of individuals being kept; and hence this comes to be of the highest importance to success.
claims.scope: artificial selection on domesticated animals and plants
measurable_quantities: response to selection as a function of population size
number of novel variants per generation versus population size
claims.candidate_data: Selection experiments varying population size (Drosophila and mouse selection lines on Dryad) and experimental-evolution data such as the LTEE.

claims.section: Summary
claims.label: Accumulative selection is the predominant cause of change in domestic races
claims.claim: Among the causes of change in domestic races, including conditions of life, use and disuse, correlation and crossing, the accumulative action of selection, whether methodical or unconscious, is by far the predominant power.
claims.quote: Over all these causes of Change I am convinced that the accumulative action of Selection, whether applied methodically and more quickly, or unconsciously and more slowly, but more efficiently, is by far the predominant Power.
claims.scope: domesticated animals and cultivated plants
measurable_quantities: fraction of breed differentiation attributable to selection versus drift, admixture or plasticity
claims.candidate_data: Genome-wide selection scans and admixture analyses of breeds and crops using GenBank/SRA data.

claims.section: Individual Differences
claims.label: Individual differences supply the material for natural selection
claims.claim: The slight individual differences among members of a species provide the materials that natural selection accumulates, in the same way that man accumulates individual differences in domestic productions.
claims.quote: These individual differences are highly important for us, as they afford materials for natural selection to accumulate, in the same manner as man can accumulate in any given direction individual differences in his domesticated productions.
claims.scope: species in a state of nature
measurable_quantities: heritability of individual trait differences in wild populations
response to natural selection in wild populations
claims.candidate_data: Long-term wild pedigree studies and compilations of heritability and selection estimates; experimental-evolution datasets on Dryad.

claims.section: Individual Differences
claims.label: Polymorphic genera vary in traits of no use, unfixed by selection
claims.claim: In polymorphic genera such as Rubus, Rosa and Hieracium, the inordinate variation concerns structures that are of no service or disservice to the species and so have not been seized on and made definite by natural selection.
claims.quote: I am inclined to suspect that we see in these polymorphic genera variations in points of structure which are of no service or disservice to the species, and which consequently have not been seized on and rendered definite by natural selection
claims.scope: polymorphic genera of plants, insects and brachiopods
measurable_quantities: fitness effects of the variable characters
within-genus variability of characters compared with non-polymorphic genera
claims.candidate_data: Taxonomic and trait data for apomictic plant complexes (World Flora Online, TRY plant trait database) with field fitness measurements.

claims.section: Doubtful species
claims.label: Doubtful forms of mobile animals are rare within a country but common between areas
claims.claim: Among highly locomotive animals that unite for each birth, doubtful forms ranked as species by some and varieties by others are rarely found within the same country but are common in separated areas.
claims.quote: Amongst animals which unite for each birth, and which are highly locomotive, doubtful forms, ranked by one zoologist as a species and by another as a variety, can rarely be found within the same country, but are common in separated areas.
claims.scope: highly mobile sexually reproducing animals such as birds and insects
measurable_quantities: number of contested species/subspecies pairs that are sympatric versus allopatric
claims.candidate_data: Comparison of differing taxonomies (e.g. Clements/eBird, IOC World Bird List, HBW and BirdLife checklists) with range maps from BirdLife International and GBIF occurrences.

claims.section: Doubtful species
claims.label: No clear line separates species, sub-species, varieties and individual differences
claims.claim: No clear line of demarcation exists between species and sub-species, between sub-species and well-marked varieties, or between lesser varieties and individual differences; they blend into one another in an insensible series.
claims.quote: Certainly no clear line of demarcation has as yet been drawn between species and sub-species—that is, the forms which in the opinion of some naturalists come very near to, but do not quite arrive at the rank of species; or, again, between sub-species and well-marked varieties, or between lesser varieties and individual differences.
claims.scope: plants and animals in nature
measurable_quantities: distribution of genetic or morphological distances among infraspecific and interspecific pairs
frequency of taxonomic disagreement over rank
claims.candidate_data: Sequence divergence data such as DNA barcodes in BOLD and GenBank, and taxonomic checklists with infraspecific ranks (WCVP, Catalogue of Life).

claims.section: Doubtful species
claims.label: Natural selection turns slight varieties into more distinct ones and species
claims.claim: Individual differences lead to slight varieties, these to more distinct and permanent varieties, then to sub-species and species, the passage being mainly due to natural selection accumulating structural differences in definite directions, so that a well-marked variety is an incipient species.
claims.quote: I attribute the passage of a variety, from a state in which it differs very slightly from its parent to one in which it differs more, to the action of natural selection in accumulating (as will hereafter be more fully explained) differences of structure in certain definite directions.
claims.scope: varieties and species in nature
measurable_quantities: divergence between incipient species over time
signatures of divergent selection between populations
claims.candidate_data: Population-genomic data for speciation continua in GenBank/SRA and divergence-time estimates in TimeTree.

claims.section: Doubtful species
claims.label: The term species is arbitrary and not essentially different from variety
claims.claim: The term species is given arbitrarily, for convenience, to a set of closely resembling individuals and does not differ essentially from the term variety, which is given to less distinct and more fluctuating forms.
claims.quote: I look at the term species, as one arbitrarily given for the sake of convenience to a set of individuals closely resembling each other, and that it does not essentially differ from the term variety, which is given to less distinct and more fluctuating forms.
claims.scope: taxonomic practice for all organisms
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Wide ranging, much diffused, and common species vary most
claims.label: Dominant species, widespread and abundant, produce the most varieties
claims.claim: The dominant species, those that range widely over the world, are most diffused in their own country and are most numerous in individuals, most often produce well-marked varieties.
claims.quote: Hence it is the most flourishing, or, as they may be called, the dominant species,—those which range widely over the world, are the most diffused in their own country, and are the most numerous in individuals,—which oftenest produce well-marked varieties, or, as I consider them, incipient species.
claims.scope: plants in regional floras
measurable_quantities: number of recorded varieties or subspecies per species
geographic range size
local abundance or occupancy
claims.candidate_data: Infraspecific taxon counts from the World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP) or POWO combined with range and occurrence data from GBIF.

claims.section: Species of the larger genera in any country vary more than the species of the smaller genera
claims.label: Species of larger genera more often present varieties
claims.claim: Within a country, a larger proportion of the species in larger genera present varieties than of the species in smaller genera, and those that vary have on average more varieties.
claims.quote: it has invariably proved to be the case that a larger proportion of the species on the side of the larger genera present varieties, than on the side of the smaller genera.
claims.scope: plants of regional floras and beetles of local faunas
measurable_quantities: proportion of species with recorded varieties by genus size
mean number of varieties per varying species by genus size
claims.candidate_data: Genus sizes and infraspecific taxa from the World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP) or regional floras, and the Catalogue of Life for beetles.

claims.section: Species of the larger genera in any country vary more than the species of the smaller genera
claims.label: Small genera often grow large while large genera peak, decline and vanish
claims.claim: Over geological time small genera have often increased greatly in number of species, and large genera have often reached a maximum, declined and disappeared.
claims.quote: geology plainly tells us that small genera have in the lapse of time often increased greatly in size; and that large genera have often come to their maxima, declined, and disappeared.
claims.scope: genera in the fossil record
measurable_quantities: species richness of genera through time
genus duration and trajectory of richness before extinction
claims.candidate_data: Fossil occurrence data from the Paleobiology Database.

claims.section: Species of the larger genera in any country vary more than the species of the smaller genera
claims.label: Where many species of a genus have formed, many are still forming
claims.claim: On the view that species are strongly marked varieties, where many species of a genus have been formed, on average many new species should still be forming.
claims.quote: All that we want to show is, that where many species of a genus have been formed, on an average many are still forming; and this holds good.
claims.scope: genera of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: recent speciation rate per clade
clade species richness
claims.candidate_data: Time-calibrated phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree) for estimating tip speciation rates against clade richness.

claims.section: Many of the species of the larger genera resemble varieties in being very closely, but unequally, related to each other, and in having restricted ranges
claims.label: Species in large genera differ from one another by small amounts
claims.claim: In large genera the amount of difference between species is often exceedingly small, so that their species resemble varieties more than do species of small genera.
claims.quote: Now Fries has remarked in regard to plants, and Westwood in regard to insects, that in large genera the amount of difference between the species is often exceedingly small. I have endeavoured to test this numerically by averages, and, as far as my imperfect results go, they always confirm the view.
claims.scope: plant and insect genera
measurable_quantities: mean pairwise morphological or genetic distance among congeners as a function of genus size
claims.candidate_data: Sequence data (GenBank, BOLD) and trait data (TRY plant trait database) analysed against genus sizes from WCVP or Catalogue of Life.

claims.section: Many of the species of the larger genera resemble varieties in being very closely, but unequally, related to each other, and in having restricted ranges
claims.label: Species of large genera cluster unequally around certain species
claims.claim: Species of large genera are not equally distinct from one another but are clustered in little groups around certain other species, as varieties are clustered around their parent species.
claims.quote: As Fries has well remarked, little groups of species are generally clustered like satellites around certain other species.
claims.scope: species within large genera
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic tree balance and clustering of species within genera
variance of pairwise distances among congeners
claims.candidate_data: Species-level phylogenies from Open Tree of Life and TimeTree, and GenBank sequence data.

claims.section: Many of the species of the larger genera resemble varieties in being very closely, but unequally, related to each other, and in having restricted ranges
claims.label: Species very closely allied to others have restricted ranges, like varieties
claims.claim: Species that are very closely allied to other species, and so resemble varieties, often have much restricted ranges, similar to the restricted ranges of acknowledged varieties.
claims.quote: But there is also reason to believe, that those species which are very closely allied to other species, and in so far resemble varieties, often have much restricted ranges.
claims.scope: plants (British flora), extended to species generally
measurable_quantities: range size of species as a function of genetic or morphological distance to nearest relative
range size of varieties versus their parent species
claims.candidate_data: Occurrence data from GBIF and range maps combined with phylogenies from Open Tree of Life or GenBank sequence data.

claims.section: Summary
claims.label: Analogies between species of large genera and varieties support descent
claims.claim: The analogies between species of large genera and varieties (more varieties, small and unequal differences, restricted ranges) are understandable if species once existed as varieties, and inexplicable if each species was independently created.
claims.quote: And we can clearly understand these analogies, if species have once existed as varieties, and have thus originated: whereas, these analogies are utterly inexplicable if each species has been independently created.
claims.scope: species and varieties of plants and animals
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Summary
claims.label: Larger genera tend to grow larger and dominant forms more dominant
claims.claim: Because the dominant species of larger genera vary most and varieties become new species, larger genera tend to become larger, and dominant forms tend to become more dominant by leaving many modified, dominant descendants.
claims.quote: The larger genera thus tend to become larger; and throughout nature the forms of life which are now dominant tend to become still more dominant by leaving many modified and dominant descendants.
claims.scope: genera and dominant species throughout nature
measurable_quantities: correlation between clade size and diversification rate
number of descendant species from widespread versus restricted ancestors
claims.candidate_data: Time-calibrated phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree) and fossil genus richness trajectories in the Paleobiology Database.

claims.section: Geometrical powers of increase
claims.label: Overproduction makes a struggle for existence inevitable
claims.claim: Because all organisms tend to increase at a high (geometrical) rate, more individuals are produced than can survive, so every species must undergo a struggle for existence with members of its own species, with other species, or with physical conditions.
claims.quote: A struggle for existence inevitably follows from the high rate at which all organic beings tend to increase.
claims.scope: all plants and animals in a state of nature
measurable_quantities: intrinsic rate of increase
fecundity
proportion of offspring surviving to reproduce
population growth rate over time
claims.candidate_data: Demographic life-table databases such as COMPADRE and COMADRE, AnAge life-history data, and long-term population time series such as the Global Population Dynamics Database.

claims.section: Rapid increase of naturalised animals and plants
claims.label: Geometrical increase explains rapid spread of naturalised species
claims.claim: The extraordinarily rapid increase and wide spread of introduced (naturalised) animals and plants in new countries is explained by geometrical increase under favourable conditions with reduced mortality, not by any rise in their fertility.
claims.quote: In such cases the geometrical ratio of increase, the result of which never fails to be surprising, simply explains the extraordinarily rapid increase and wide diffusion of naturalised productions in their new homes.
claims.scope: introduced and feral animals and plants
measurable_quantities: population growth rate of introduced species after arrival
range expansion rate
fecundity in native versus introduced range
juvenile survival in native versus introduced range
claims.candidate_data: Naturalised-flora and invasion databases (GloNAF, GBIF occurrence time series) combined with native-versus-introduced range demographic comparisons in the published literature.

claims.section: Geometrical powers of increase
claims.label: Average abundance depends only indirectly on fecundity
claims.claim: The average number of individuals of an animal or plant species depends only indirectly on how many eggs or seeds it produces; high fecundity mainly compensates for heavy destruction, usually early in life.
claims.quote: So that in all cases, the average number of any animal or plant depends only indirectly on the number of its eggs or seeds.
claims.scope: all animals and plants
measurable_quantities: clutch size or seed output per individual
population abundance or density
early-life mortality rate
parental care
claims.candidate_data: Life-history trait compilations (AnAge, AVONET, TRY plant traits, FishBase) combined with abundance estimates (e.g. global bird population estimates, BioTIME, GBIF).

claims.section: Nature of the checks to increase
claims.label: Predation, more often than food supply, sets average numbers
claims.claim: Although food sets the upper limit to a species' increase, very often it is destruction by predators rather than food supply that determines the species' average numbers.
claims.quote: The amount of food for each species of course gives the extreme limit to which each can increase; but very frequently it is not the obtaining food, but the serving as prey to other animals, which determines the average numbers of a species.
claims.scope: animal populations in nature, e.g. game birds and mammals
measurable_quantities: population density with and without predator removal
population response to food supplementation
predation mortality rate
claims.candidate_data: Predator-removal and food-supplementation field experiments compiled in meta-analyses (data often deposited in Dryad), and long-term predator-prey time series such as the Global Population Dynamics Database.

claims.section: Effects of climate
claims.label: Periodic extreme cold or drought is the most effective check
claims.claim: Climate plays an important part in determining the average numbers of a species, and periodic seasons of extreme cold or drought are the most effective of all checks on increase.
claims.quote: Climate plays an important part in determining the average numbers of a species, and periodical seasons of extreme cold or drought, I believe to be the most effective of all checks.
claims.scope: animal and plant populations, e.g. birds in severe winters
measurable_quantities: population change across extreme climatic events
mortality during severe winters or droughts
relative contribution of climate versus biotic factors to population fluctuations
claims.candidate_data: Long-term bird monitoring (North American Breeding Bird Survey, Pan-European Common Bird Monitoring Scheme), BioTIME and Living Planet Index time series matched to climate records such as ERA5 or CRU.

claims.section: Effects of climate
claims.label: Competitors decline poleward, so climate acts more directly there
claims.claim: The number of species, and therefore of competitors, decreases going northward, so that going north or up a mountain one more often finds stunted forms caused by the direct harmful action of climate than going south or downhill.
claims.quote: for the number of species of all kinds, and therefore of competitors, decreases northwards; hence in going northward, or in ascending a mountain, we far oftener meet with stunted forms, due to the _directly_ injurious action of climate, than we do in proceeding southwards or in descending a mountain.
claims.scope: plants and animals along latitudinal and elevational gradients
measurable_quantities: species richness along latitude and elevation
frequency of stunted growth forms
relative importance of abiotic versus biotic range limits
claims.candidate_data: GBIF and BIEN occurrence data for richness gradients, sPlot vegetation plots and TRY plant height data along gradients, with climate layers such as WorldClim or CHELSA.

claims.section: Effects of climate
claims.label: Climate limits species mainly indirectly, by favouring competitors
claims.claim: Climate limits species mainly indirectly, by favouring their competitors and enemies; for example, many garden plants that tolerate the local climate never become naturalised because they cannot compete with native plants or resist native animals.
claims.quote: That climate acts in main part indirectly by favouring other species, we may clearly see in the prodigious number of plants in our gardens which can perfectly well endure our climate, but which never become naturalised, for they cannot compete with our native plants, nor resist destruction by our native animals.
claims.scope: plants, especially cultivated exotics and native floras
measurable_quantities: fraction of cultivated exotic species that naturalise
climatic match between cultivation sites and native range
establishment success with and without competitors or herbivores
claims.candidate_data: GloNAF naturalised-flora data compared with horticultural species lists and climate-niche data from GBIF and WorldClim, plus competitor- and herbivore-removal experiments.

claims.section: Protection from the number of individuals
claims.label: Many species need a large local stock to persist
claims.claim: In many cases a large number of individuals of a species, relative to the number of its enemies, is necessary for the species to survive, which explains why rare plants can be very abundant in the few spots where they occur.
claims.quote: On the other hand, in many cases, a large stock of individuals of the same species, relatively to the numbers of its enemies, is absolutely necessary for its preservation.
claims.scope: plants and animals subject to predation, e.g. seed crops eaten by birds
measurable_quantities: per-capita survival or seed loss versus local population size
minimum viable population density
local abundance of rare species where present
claims.candidate_data: Published Allee-effect and predator-satiation studies, and population time series in the Global Population Dynamics Database and COMPADRE.

claims.section: Complex relations of all animals and plants throughout nature
claims.label: Balanced struggles keep communities uniform over long periods
claims.claim: Although competition between organisms constantly recurs with shifting outcomes, the opposing forces are so finely balanced that community composition stays roughly the same for long periods, even though a trifling change could tip the balance toward one organism.
claims.quote: Battle within battle must ever be recurring with varying success; and yet in the long-run the forces are so nicely balanced, that the face of nature remains uniform for long periods of time, though assuredly the merest trifle would often give the victory to one organic being over another.
claims.scope: natural communities of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: temporal turnover in species composition
variance in relative abundances over time
community stability metrics
claims.candidate_data: Long-term community time series in BioTIME, the US LTER network, and pollen records from the Neotoma Paleoecology Database.

claims.section: Complex relations of all animals and plants throughout nature
claims.label: Chains of interaction link distant species' abundances
claims.claim: Very different organisms are linked by chains of interaction, so that the abundance of one species can determine the frequency of another through intermediate species; for example, cats may control the frequency of red clover and heartsease by way of field-mice and humble-bees.
claims.quote: Hence it is quite credible that the presence of a feline animal in large numbers in a district might determine, through the intervention first of mice and then of bees, the frequency of certain flowers in that district!
claims.scope: terrestrial communities of plants, pollinators, and their predators
measurable_quantities: predator density
rodent density
bumblebee nest density
seed set and abundance of bee-pollinated plants
claims.candidate_data: Interaction-network data (GloBI, Web of Life), published trophic-cascade field studies, and bumblebee and plant monitoring data from GBIF.

claims.section: Struggle for life most severe between individuals and varieties of the same species; often severe between species of the same genus
claims.label: Struggle is most severe between members of the same species
claims.claim: The struggle for existence is almost always most severe between individuals of the same species, because they live in the same places, need the same food and face the same dangers; between varieties of a species it is nearly as severe.
claims.quote: But the struggle almost invariably will be most severe between the individuals of the same species, for they frequent the same districts, require the same food, and are exposed to the same dangers.
claims.scope: all organisms, including varieties of cultivated plants and domestic animals
measurable_quantities: strength of intraspecific versus interspecific competition coefficients
per-capita effects of conspecific versus heterospecific density on growth or survival
claims.candidate_data: Meta-analyses of competition experiments and plant neighbourhood data such as ForestGEO census plots that estimate conspecific versus heterospecific density effects.

claims.section: Struggle for life most severe between individuals and varieties of the same species; often severe between species of the same genus
claims.label: Congeners compete more severely than species of different genera
claims.claim: Because species of the same genus are usually similar in habits and constitution and always in structure, competition between them is generally more severe than between species of different genera.
claims.quote: As species of the same genus have usually, though by no means invariably, some similarity in habits and constitution, and always in structure, the struggle will generally be more severe between species of the same genus, when they come into competition with each other, than between species of distinct genera.
claims.scope: co-occurring species of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: competition strength versus phylogenetic distance
trait similarity versus relatedness
displacement of one species by a congener
claims.candidate_data: Pairwise competition experiments related to phylogenies from Open Tree of Life or TimeTree, and co-occurrence data from sPlot or GBIF.

claims.section: The relation of organism to organism the most important of all relations
claims.label: Each organism's structure is shaped by its relations to other organisms
claims.claim: The structure of every organism is related, in essential but often hidden ways, to the structure of the other organisms with which it competes, from which it must escape, or on which it preys.
claims.quote: A corollary of the highest importance may be deduced from the foregoing remarks, namely, that the structure of every organic being is related, in the most essential yet often hidden manner, to that of all other organic beings, with which it comes into competition for food or residence, or from which it has to escape, or on which it preys.
claims.scope: all organisms
measurable_quantities: trait variation explained by biotic versus abiotic factors
trait shifts in response to competitors, predators or prey
claims.candidate_data: Trait databases (TRY, AVONET) combined with interaction data (GloBI) and published character-displacement studies.

claims.section: The relation of organism to organism the most important of all relations
claims.label: Few species reach range edges where climate alone kills them
claims.claim: Only a few plants or animals extend their ranges so far that they are destroyed by the severity of climate alone; competition continues everywhere except at the extreme limits of life.
claims.quote: we have reason to believe that only a few plants or animals range so far, that they are destroyed by the rigour of the climate alone.
claims.scope: geographic range limits of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: proportion of range limits set by abiotic tolerance versus biotic interactions
performance of transplants beyond range edges with and without competitors
claims.candidate_data: Published transplant experiments beyond range limits, together with GBIF occurrence data and physiological tolerance compilations such as GlobTherm.

claims.section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
claims.label: Natural selection preserves favourable and destroys injurious variations
claims.claim: Because more individuals are born than can survive, individuals with any advantage, however slight, have the best chance of surviving and reproducing, while injurious variations are eliminated; this preservation of favourable and rejection of injurious variations is natural selection.
claims.quote: This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection.
claims.scope: all organisms in nature
measurable_quantities: selection differentials and gradients on traits
heritability of traits
differential survival and reproduction
claims.candidate_data: Compilations of selection gradients measured in wild populations, long-term field studies of wild populations, and experimental-evolution datasets such as the LTEE.

claims.section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
claims.label: Neutral variations escape selection and remain fluctuating
claims.claim: Variations that are neither useful nor harmful are not acted on by natural selection and stay variable, which may explain the variability of so-called polymorphic species.
claims.quote: Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic.
claims.scope: characters of all organisms, especially polymorphic species
measurable_quantities: fitness effect of a character
variance of the character within and among populations
temporal fluctuation of character frequencies
claims.candidate_data: Long-term studies of polymorphism frequencies in wild populations and morphological trait variance in trait databases, compared with measured selection on those traits.

claims.section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
claims.label: No native biota is so well adapted that it cannot be improved
claims.claim: No country's native inhabitants are so perfectly adapted that none could be improved, as shown by introduced species having established firmly in every country.
claims.quote: No country can be named in which all the native inhabitants are now so perfectly adapted to each other and to the physical conditions under which they live, that none of them could anyhow be improved; for in all countries, the natives have been so far conquered by naturalised productions, that they have allowed foreigners to take firm possession of the land.
claims.scope: native biotas of all countries and regions
measurable_quantities: number and share of established alien species per region
displacement of native species by aliens
claims.candidate_data: Global alien-species databases such as GloNAF, the Alien Species First Records Database, and GRIIS (Global Register of Introduced and Invasive Species).

claims.section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
claims.label: Protective colours matching backgrounds are maintained by selection
claims.claim: Seemingly trivial characters such as colour can be shaped by natural selection; colours that match the background, as in green leaf-eating insects and heather-coloured grouse, protect their bearers from predators that hunt by sight.
claims.quote: When we see leaf-eating insects green, and bark-feeders mottled-grey; the alpine ptarmigan white in winter, the red-grouse the colour of heather, and the black-grouse that of peaty earth, we must believe that these tints are of service to these birds and insects in preserving them from danger.
claims.scope: animals preyed on by visually hunting predators
measurable_quantities: background matching of coloration
predation rate on matching versus mismatching morphs
coloration versus habitat across species
claims.candidate_data: Field predation experiments on cryptic versus conspicuous prey models, comparative plumage-colour datasets from museum specimens, and long-term morph-frequency records such as those for the peppered moth.

claims.section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
claims.label: Natural selection can modify organisms at any age
claims.claim: Because variations arising at a particular life stage tend to be inherited at the same stage, natural selection can modify organisms at any age, for instance adapting larvae independently of adults.
claims.quote: natural selection will be enabled to act on and modify organic beings at any age, by the accumulation of profitable variations at that age, and by their inheritance at a corresponding age.
claims.scope: all organisms, especially those with distinct life stages such as insects with larvae
measurable_quantities: selection on juvenile versus adult traits
trait correlations between life stages
stage-specific heritability
claims.candidate_data: Studies of stage-specific selection and morphological decoupling between larvae and adults in insects and amphibians, with phylogenies from Open Tree of Life.

claims.section: Sexual Selection
claims.label: Males of polygamous species fight most and carry special weapons
claims.claim: Fighting between males for females is perhaps most severe in polygamous animals, and the males of such species are the most often equipped with special weapons.
claims.quote: The war is, perhaps, severest between the males of polygamous animals, and these seem oftenest provided with special weapons.
claims.scope: animals with male-male competition for mates, especially mammals and birds
measurable_quantities: mating system (degree of polygyny)
male weapon size or presence
sexual size dimorphism
intensity of male-male combat
claims.candidate_data: Comparative mating-system and morphology data such as PanTHERIA, AVONET and published sexual-dimorphism compilations, analysed on phylogenies from BirdTree or VertLife.

claims.section: Sexual Selection
claims.label: Female choice over many generations can produce male ornaments
claims.claim: Female birds, by choosing the most melodious or beautiful males over thousands of generations, can produce a marked change in male song or plumage.
claims.quote: I can see no good reason to doubt that female birds, by selecting, during thousands of generations, the most melodious or beautiful males, according to their standard of beauty, might produce a marked effect.
claims.scope: birds, especially species with male display
measurable_quantities: female preference for male song or plumage traits
mating success versus ornament expression
ornament evolution across lineages
claims.candidate_data: Mate-choice experiments and field mating-success studies in birds, together with plumage and song comparative datasets analysed on BirdTree phylogenies.

claims.section: Sexual Selection
claims.label: Sex differences in species with shared habits are mainly sexually selected
claims.claim: When males and females of a species share the same general habits of life but differ in structure, colour or ornament, those differences were mainly caused by sexual selection, although not all such differences are.
claims.quote: Thus it is, as I believe, that when the males and females of any animal have the same general habits of life, but differ in structure, colour, or ornament, such differences have been mainly caused by sexual selection
claims.scope: sexually dimorphic animals
measurable_quantities: degree of sexual dimorphism
measures of sexual selection intensity (mating system, variance in male mating success)
ecological differences between sexes
claims.candidate_data: Comparative sexual-dimorphism and mating-system data (e.g. AVONET, PanTHERIA, published bird plumage dichromatism scores) analysed on phylogenies.

claims.section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
claims.label: Flowers and their insect visitors become mutually adapted
claims.claim: A flower and a bee can slowly become modified and adapted to each other, at the same time or one after the other, by the continued preservation of individuals with mutually favourable slight differences in structure.
claims.quote: Thus I can understand how a flower and a bee might slowly become, either simultaneously or one after the other, modified and adapted in the most perfect manner to each other, by the continued preservation of individuals presenting mutual and slightly favourable deviations of structure.
claims.scope: flowering plants and their insect pollinators
measurable_quantities: corolla tube length
pollinator proboscis length
trait matching across plant-pollinator pairs
pollination success versus trait match
claims.candidate_data: Plant-pollinator interaction networks (Web of Life, GloBI) with floral and pollinator trait data, and published studies on correlated tube and tongue lengths.

claims.section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
claims.label: Natural selection works only by accumulating very small modifications
claims.claim: Natural selection acts only by preserving and accumulating very small inherited modifications, each profitable to its bearer, and so excludes continued creation of new organisms or large sudden changes of structure.
claims.quote: Natural selection can act only by the preservation and accumulation of infinitesimally small inherited modifications, each profitable to the preserved being
claims.scope: all organisms
measurable_quantities: distribution of effect sizes of adaptive changes
rates of morphological change between successive generations or fossil samples
claims.candidate_data: Experimental-evolution datasets (e.g. LTEE) and fine-scale fossil sequences in the Paleobiology Database that record morphological change over time.

claims.section: On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species
claims.label: Crossing increases vigour; close interbreeding decreases it
claims.claim: In animals and plants, crosses between different varieties or between different strains of the same variety give vigour and fertility to the offspring, while close interbreeding reduces vigour and fertility.
claims.quote: a cross between different varieties, or between individuals of the same variety but of another strain, gives vigour and fertility to the offspring; and on the other hand, that _close_ interbreeding diminishes vigour and fertility
claims.scope: animals and plants, wild and domestic
measurable_quantities: offspring survival and fertility from outcrosses versus inbred matings
inbreeding depression
heterosis
claims.candidate_data: Meta-analyses of inbreeding depression and heterosis in wild and domestic populations, and pedigreed long-term wild-population and livestock breeding records.

claims.section: On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species
claims.label: No organism self-fertilises indefinitely; occasional crosses are needed
claims.claim: It is a general law of nature that no organism fertilises itself for an unlimited number of generations; an occasional cross with another individual, perhaps at long intervals, is indispensable, even in hermaphrodites.
claims.quote: it is a general law of nature (utterly ignorant though we be of the meaning of the law) that no organic being self-fertilises itself for an eternity of generations; but that a cross with another individual is occasionally—perhaps at very long intervals—indispensable.
claims.scope: all plants and animals, especially hermaphrodites
measurable_quantities: outcrossing rate
persistence and diversification rate of selfing or asexual lineages
longevity of exclusively selfing lineages
claims.candidate_data: Plant mating-system compilations (outcrossing-rate databases in the literature), phylogenetic studies of selfing and asexual lineage age using TimeTree or Open Tree of Life.

claims.section: On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species
claims.label: Trees more often have separate sexes than other plants
claims.claim: Trees, across all plant orders, have separate male and female flowers more often than other plants do, which helps pollen move between trees (though Hooker reported the rule fails in Australia).
claims.quote: That trees belonging to all Orders have their sexes more often separated than other plants, I find to be the case in this country
claims.scope: flowering plants, comparing trees with non-woody plants
measurable_quantities: frequency of dioecy and monoecy in trees versus herbs
growth form
claims.candidate_data: Plant sexual-system and growth-form data from the Tree of Sex database, TRY, and regional floras, analysed on Open Tree of Life phylogenies.

claims.section: Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals
claims.label: Large populations favour natural selection by supplying more variations
claims.claim: A large number of individuals favours natural selection because it gives a better chance for profitable variations to arise within a given period, compensating for lower variability in each individual.
claims.quote: A large number of individuals, by giving a better chance for the appearance within any given period of profitable variations, will compensate for a lesser amount of variability in each individual, and is, I believe, an extremely important element of success.
claims.scope: all species undergoing natural selection
measurable_quantities: population size
rate of adaptation
rate of appearance of beneficial variants
claims.candidate_data: Experimental-evolution studies that manipulate population size (e.g. microbial evolution datasets deposited in Dryad) and comparative studies of adaptation rate versus population size.

claims.section: Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals
claims.label: Large areas produce more, faster-forming and wider-spreading new species
claims.claim: Although small isolated areas can favour new species, modification is generally faster on large areas, and forms produced there, having beaten many competitors, spread most widely and give rise to the most new varieties and species.
claims.quote: Finally, I conclude that, although small isolated areas probably have been in some respects highly favourable for the production of new species, yet that the course of modification will generally have been more rapid on large areas; and what is more important, that the new forms produced on large areas, which already have been victorious over many competitors, will be those that will spread most widely
claims.scope: terrestrial species in continents versus islands and small regions
measurable_quantities: speciation or diversification rate versus area
range size and spread of lineages originating in large versus small areas
claims.candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree, BirdTree) combined with biogeographic range data (GBIF, IUCN range maps) to estimate diversification rates by region area.

claims.section: Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals
claims.label: Freshwater biotas evolve and go extinct more slowly, keeping relict forms
claims.claim: Because all freshwater basins together form a small area, competition among freshwater organisms has been less severe, so new forms have arisen more slowly and old forms have been exterminated more slowly there, which is why fresh water holds ancient and anomalous forms.
claims.quote: All fresh-water basins, taken together, make a small area compared with that of the sea or of the land; and, consequently, the competition between fresh-water productions will have been less severe than elsewhere; new forms will have been more slowly formed, and old forms more slowly exterminated.
claims.scope: freshwater organisms, compared with marine and terrestrial ones
measurable_quantities: origination and extinction rates of freshwater versus marine or terrestrial lineages
frequency of relict (living-fossil) lineages by habitat
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database origination and extinction rates by environment, and dated fish phylogenies (e.g. Fish Tree of Life) for diversification by habitat.

claims.section: Slow action
claims.label: Natural selection acts slowly, intermittently and on few species at a time
claims.claim: Natural selection always acts very slowly, often only at long intervals of time, and generally on only a very few of the inhabitants of a region at the same time.
claims.quote: On the other hand, I do believe that natural selection will always act very slowly, often only at long intervals of time, and generally on only a very few of the inhabitants of the same region at the same time.
claims.scope: all organisms within a region over geological time
measurable_quantities: rates of morphological change in fossil lineages
proportion of lineages changing in a given interval
evolutionary stasis versus change in fossil series
claims.candidate_data: Fossil time series and occurrence data in the Paleobiology Database and Neotoma, and compilations of evolutionary rates across timescales.

claims.section: Extinction caused by Natural Selection
claims.label: Favoured forms make less favoured forms rare, and rarity precedes extinction
claims.claim: Because every area is already fully stocked, as a favoured form increases in number the less favoured forms decrease and become rare, and rarity precedes extinction.
claims.quote: it follows that as each selected and favoured form increases in number, so will the less favoured forms decrease and become rare. Rarity, as geology tells us, is the precursor to extinction.
claims.scope: species in fully occupied areas, over ecological and geological time
measurable_quantities: abundance or occupancy decline before extinction
abundance trends of competing species
extinction risk versus rarity
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occupancy trajectories before extinction, IUCN Red List assessments, and the Living Planet Index abundance trends.

claims.section: Extinction caused by Natural Selection
claims.label: New forms press hardest on and tend to exterminate their nearest relatives
claims.claim: Because the most closely related forms compete most severely, each new variety or species, while forming, presses hardest on its nearest relatives and tends to exterminate them.
claims.quote: Consequently, each new variety or species, during the progress of its formation, will generally press hardest on its nearest kindred, and tend to exterminate them.
claims.scope: varieties and species, wild and domesticated
measurable_quantities: extinction of a lineage in relation to origination of close relatives
phylogenetic clustering of extinctions
replacement of older breeds or varieties by newer ones
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database origination and extinction data analysed for clade replacement, dated phylogenies (TimeTree), and historical records of livestock breed replacement such as FAO DAD-IS.

claims.section: Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation
claims.label: Divergence of character maximises the life an area supports
claims.claim: The greatest amount of life can be supported in an area by great diversification of structure among its inhabitants.
claims.quote: The truth of the principle, that the greatest amount of life can be supported by great diversification of structure, is seen under many natural circumstances.
claims.scope: local communities of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: species or genus richness per unit area
biomass or individual density per unit area
claims.candidate_data: Plot-level biodiversity-productivity experiments (e.g. Cedar Creek BigBio, Jena Experiment); sPlot vegetation plots

claims.section: Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation
claims.label: The closest-competing neighbours tend to belong to different genera and orders
claims.claim: Where organisms compete most closely, as on a small patch of ground, the advantages of diversification mean that the coexisting inhabitants generally belong to different genera and orders.
claims.quote: where they come into the closest competition with each other, the advantages of diversification of structure, with the accompanying differences of habit and constitution, determine that the inhabitants, which thus jostle each other most closely, shall, as a general rule, belong to what we call different genera and orders.
claims.scope: small-area communities, e.g. turf plots, islets, small ponds
measurable_quantities: genera-to-species and orders-to-species ratios in small plots versus regional pools
phylogenetic dispersion of local communities
claims.candidate_data: Vegetation plot databases (sPlot, BIEN plots) with phylogenies from Open Tree of Life to compute phylogenetic over- or under-dispersion.

claims.section: Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation
claims.label: Naturalised floras add proportionally more new genera than new species
claims.claim: Floras gain far more new genera than new species from naturalised plants, relative to the native numbers of genera and species, so naturalised plants tend to differ from the natives at the genus level.
claims.quote: floras gain by naturalisation, proportionally with the number of the native genera and species, far more in new genera than in new species.
claims.scope: naturalised plants in regional floras
measurable_quantities: proportion of naturalised species in genera absent from the native flora
species-to-genus ratio of naturalised versus native floras
phylogenetic distance of naturalised species to natives
claims.candidate_data: GloNAF naturalised-flora checklists compared with native floras, with phylogenetic distances from Open Tree of Life.

claims.section: Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent
claims.label: Intermediate forms and parent species tend to go extinct
claims.claim: In a fully stocked country, improved descendants of a species tend to supplant their predecessors, so the intermediate forms between earlier and later states, and the original parent species itself, generally tend to become extinct.
claims.quote: Hence all the intermediate forms between the earlier and later states, that is between the less and more improved state of a species, as well as the original parent-species itself, will generally tend to become extinct.
claims.scope: lineages of species descended from a common parent
measurable_quantities: persistence of ancestral morphotypes alongside descendants
frequency of budding versus anagenetic replacement in fossil lineages
survival of intermediate morphologies
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrence data and published ancestor-descendant fossil series (e.g. planktonic foraminifera lineage data).

claims.section: Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent
claims.label: Extinct species are often intermediate between living groups
claims.claim: Extinct species, though generally in the same orders, families or genera as living ones, are often somewhat intermediate in character between existing groups, because they lived when the branching lines of descent had diverged less.
claims.quote: the diagram throws light on the affinities of extinct beings, which, though generally belonging to the same orders, or families, or genera, with those now living, yet are often, in some degree, intermediate in character between existing groups
claims.scope: fossil and living species of all groups
measurable_quantities: morphological position of fossil taxa relative to living groups
phylogenetic placement of fossils (stem versus crown)
disparity between groups through time
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database taxonomy, morphological character matrices in MorphoBank, and phylogenies including fossils in Open Tree of Life.

claims.section: Summary
claims.label: Differences between varieties grow into differences between species and genera
claims.claim: Through natural selection and divergence of character, the small differences between varieties of a species steadily increase until they equal the larger differences between species of the same genus, or even between genera.
claims.quote: Thus the small differences distinguishing varieties of the same species, will steadily tend to increase till they come to equal the greater differences between species of the same genus, or even of distinct genera.
claims.scope: varieties, species and genera of all organisms
measurable_quantities: phenotypic divergence versus time since divergence
divergence of within-species varieties compared with between-species differences
claims.candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree) combined with trait data (AVONET, TRY) to relate trait divergence to divergence time, and fossil series in the Paleobiology Database.

claims.section: Summary
claims.label: Very few species of past periods have living descendants
claims.claim: Like a tree in which only a few early twigs grew into surviving branches, very few of the species that lived in long-past geological periods now have living modified descendants, and many whole orders, families and genera have died out entirely.
claims.quote: Of the many twigs which flourished when the tree was a mere bush, only two or three, now grown into great branches, yet survive and bear all the other branches; so with the species which lived during long-past geological periods, very few now have living and modified descendants.
claims.scope: all lineages over geological time
measurable_quantities: fraction of species or clades in a past interval with living descendants
clade extinction rates
shape of phylogenies including fossils
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrence and range data, combined with time-calibrated phylogenies from TimeTree and Open Tree of Life.

claims.section: Effects of external conditions.
claims.label: Variability is induced by changed conditions acting on the reproductive system
claims.claim: Deviations of structure arise in some way from the conditions of life to which parents and their ancestors have been exposed over several generations, acting chiefly by disturbing the reproductive system; hence variability is greater under domestication or cultivation than in nature.
claims.quote: But the much greater variability, as well as the greater frequency of monstrosities, under domestication or cultivation, than under nature, leads me to believe that deviations of structure are in some way due to the nature of the conditions of life, to which the parents and their more remote ancestors have been exposed during several generations.
claims.scope: plants and animals, domesticated and wild
measurable_quantities: phenotypic variance of domesticated vs wild conspecifics
frequency of developmental abnormalities under captive vs wild conditions
variance in offspring traits after environmental change of parents
claims.candidate_data: Comparative morphometric datasets of domestic breeds and their wild ancestors (e.g. dog and pigeon morphometrics on Dryad); plant common-garden and transplant experiments.

claims.section: Effects of external conditions.
claims.label: Direct effects of climate and food on organisms are small
claims.claim: The direct effect of differences in climate, food and similar conditions on an organism's structure is very small in animals and perhaps somewhat larger in plants, and cannot account for the complex co-adaptations between organisms.
claims.quote: How much direct effect difference of climate, food, etc., produces on any being is extremely doubtful. My impression is, that the effect is extremely small in the case of animals, but perhaps rather more in that of plants.
claims.scope: plants and animals in nature
measurable_quantities: magnitude of phenotypic plasticity in response to temperature or diet
plasticity effect sizes in animals vs plants
claims.candidate_data: Meta-analytic datasets of phenotypic plasticity from reciprocal-transplant and common-garden experiments, many archived on Dryad; TRY plant trait database for within-species trait variation across environments.

claims.section: Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.
claims.label: Flightlessness of birds on predator-free oceanic islands is caused by disuse
claims.claim: The nearly wingless condition of several birds living on oceanic islands that lack beasts of prey has been caused by disuse of the wings.
claims.quote: I believe that the nearly wingless condition of several birds, which now inhabit or have lately inhabited several oceanic islands, tenanted by no beast of prey, has been caused by disuse.
claims.scope: birds of oceanic islands
measurable_quantities: incidence of flightlessness on islands with vs without mammalian predators
relative wing size in island vs mainland relatives
claims.candidate_data: AVONET avian morphology database and bird phylogenies (BirdTree) for island vs mainland wing-length comparisons; subfossil records of extinct flightless island birds.

claims.section: Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.
claims.label: Wingless Madeira beetles result mainly from selection against being blown to sea
claims.claim: The high proportion of flightless beetles on windswept islands such as Madeira is mainly due to natural selection favouring individuals that fly least and so avoid being blown out to sea, probably combined with disuse.
claims.quote: these several considerations have made me believe that the wingless condition of so many Madeira beetles is mainly due to the action of natural selection, but combined probably with disuse.
claims.scope: insects of oceanic islands, especially ground-living beetles
measurable_quantities: proportion of flightless insect species per island
wind exposure of islands
wing reduction in ground-feeding vs flower-feeding island insects
