phylogenetic clustering of extinction
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrences mapped onto phylogenies, and phylogenetic signal analyses of extinction risk using IUCN Red List and Open Tree of Life.

claims.section: On simultaneous changes in the forms of life throughout the world
claims.label: Marine forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world
claims.claim: The forms of marine life change almost simultaneously, in a broad geological sense, throughout the world, so that formations in distant regions under different climates can be correlated by their fossils.
claims.quote: Scarcely any palæontological discovery is more striking than the fact, that the forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world.
claims.scope: marine faunas across continents and climates
measurable_quantities: synchrony of first and last appearances across regions
faunal similarity between contemporaneous distant assemblages
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database and Neptune occurrences with independent (radiometric or magnetostratigraphic) age control.

claims.section: On the affinities of extinct species to each other and to living species
claims.label: The more ancient a form, the more it differs from living forms
claims.claim: As a general rule, the older a fossil form is, the more it differs from living forms.
claims.quote: The more ancient any form is, the more, as a general rule, it differs from living forms.
claims.scope: fossil species and genera compared with living relatives
measurable_quantities: morphological distance from nearest living relative as a function of fossil age
proportion of extant genera in assemblages by age
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database (proportion of extant taxa by age) and morphological character matrices from MorphoBank.

claims.section: On the affinities of extinct species to each other and to living species
claims.label: Extinct forms fill gaps between existing genera, families and orders
claims.claim: All fossils can be classed in existing groups or between them, and extinct forms fill up the wide intervals between existing genera, families and orders, forming with living forms one natural system.
claims.quote: That the extinct forms of life help to fill up the wide intervals between existing genera, families, and orders, cannot be disputed.
claims.scope: all extinct and living organisms
measurable_quantities: placement of fossil taxa on phylogenies relative to living clades
reduction in branch lengths/gaps when fossils are included
claims.candidate_data: Open Tree of Life and published total-evidence phylogenies combining fossil and living taxa (e.g. MorphoBank matrices).

claims.section: On the affinities of extinct species to each other and to living species
claims.label: Older members of distinct groups differ less from each other than living members
claims.claim: Groups that have changed much over known geological periods should, in older formations, approach each other slightly, so that their older members differ from each other in fewer characters than their living members do.
claims.quote: All that we have a right to expect, is that those groups, which have within known geological periods undergone much modification, should in the older formations make some slight approach to each other; so that the older members should differ less from each other in some of their characters than do the existing members of the same groups
claims.scope: pairs of related higher groups (e.g. fish and reptiles) across geological time
measurable_quantities: morphological distance between members of two groups as a function of geological age
number of diagnostic characters separating groups over time
claims.candidate_data: Morphological disparity analyses on character matrices (e.g. MorphoBank) combined with Paleobiology Database ages.

claims.section: On the affinities of extinct species to each other and to living species
claims.label: Fossils from consecutive formations are more alike than those from remote ones
claims.claim: Fossils from two consecutive formations are far more closely related to each other than fossils from two formations widely separated in time, and the fauna of each period is broadly intermediate between those before and after it.
claims.quote: fossils from two consecutive formations are far more closely related to each other, than are the fossils from two remote formations.
claims.scope: fossil faunas in successive geological formations
measurable_quantities: taxonomic similarity between assemblages as a function of time separation
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database assemblage data for faunal similarity-decay analyses.

claims.section: On the state of development of ancient forms
claims.label: Later faunas would outcompete earlier faunas under similar conditions
claims.claim: Because each new species arose by having some advantage over preceding forms, a more recent fauna or flora would beat and exterminate an older one if they were placed in competition under a similar climate, and in this sense recent forms are higher.
claims.quote: If under a nearly similar climate, the eocene inhabitants of one quarter of the world were put into competition with the existing inhabitants of the same or some other quarter, the eocene fauna or flora would certainly be beaten and exterminated
claims.scope: faunas and floras of successive geological periods
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: On the succession of the same types within the same areas
claims.label: Each region's fossils are succeeded by allied living forms in the same region
claims.claim: Within the same continent or area, the extinct forms of the later Tertiary are closely allied to the living inhabitants (e.g. fossil and living marsupials in Australia, edentates in South America), because each area's inhabitants leave modified descendants there.
claims.quote: the great law of the long enduring, but not immutable, succession of the same types within the same areas, is at once explained; for the inhabitants of each quarter of the world will obviously tend to leave in that quarter, during the next succeeding period of time, closely allied though in some degree modified descendants.
claims.scope: terrestrial mammals, birds and molluscs of continents and islands in the later Tertiary
measurable_quantities: taxonomic affinity of regional late-Cenozoic fossils to living regional versus extra-regional faunas
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database and NOW fossil mammal database occurrences compared with living distributions in GBIF.

claims.section: Present distribution cannot be accounted for by differences in physical conditions
claims.label: Physical conditions do not explain the similarity or dissimilarity of regional biotas
claims.claim: Neither the similarity nor the dissimilarity of the inhabitants of different regions can be explained by their climate and other physical conditions; regions with closely parallel conditions (e.g. Australia, South Africa and western South America at 25°–35° S) have utterly different faunas and floras.
claims.quote: the first great fact which strikes us is, that neither the similarity nor the dissimilarity of the inhabitants of various regions can be accounted for by their climatal and other physical conditions.
claims.scope: terrestrial and marine faunas and floras of the world's major regions
measurable_quantities: compositional (taxonomic or phylogenetic) similarity between regions
climatic/environmental similarity between regions
claims.candidate_data: Species occurrence data from GBIF and OBIS combined with WorldClim climate layers, and phylogenies from Open Tree of Life, allow partitioning biotic similarity into climatic and geographic/historical components.

claims.section: Importance of barriers
claims.label: Barriers to migration correspond closely to differences between regional biotas
claims.claim: Barriers of any kind that obstruct free migration (oceans, isthmuses, mountain ranges, deserts, large rivers) are closely related to the differences between the inhabitants of different regions, and the more impassable and long-standing the barrier, the greater the difference.
claims.quote: A second great fact which strikes us in our general review is, that barriers of any kind, or obstacles to free migration, are related in a close and important manner to the differences between the productions of various regions.
claims.scope: terrestrial and marine organisms across continents, oceans and within continents
measurable_quantities: species turnover (beta diversity) across barriers versus across equal distances without barriers
barrier type and estimated age
claims.candidate_data: GBIF and OBIS occurrence records with biogeographic regionalisations (e.g. Holt et al. 2013 zoogeographic regions) and phylogenies from Open Tree of Life or TimeTree, including the well-studied trans-Isthmian marine species pairs.

claims.section: Affinity of the productions of the same continent
claims.label: Species of the same continent or sea are related despite differing stations
claims.claim: The inhabitants of the same continent or sea show a pervasive affinity to one another, so that distinct but related species replace one another from place to place and across different habitats, rather than being replaced by forms from other continents living under similar conditions.
claims.quote: A third great fact, partly included in the foregoing statements, is the affinity of the productions of the same continent or sea, though the species themselves are distinct at different points and stations.
claims.scope: species assemblages within continents and seas
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic relatedness of co-continental species versus species from other continents in similar habitats
claims.candidate_data: Phylogenies from Open Tree of Life or TimeTree combined with GBIF distributions allow testing whether species are phylogenetically clustered by continent more than by habitat or climate.

claims.section: Affinity of the productions of the same continent
claims.label: The bond linking inhabitants of the same area through space and time is inheritance
claims.claim: The deep affinity uniting the living and extinct inhabitants of the same area, independent of physical conditions, is due to inheritance from common ancestors, while the differences among regions arise mainly from modification through natural selection and only subordinately from the direct influence of physical conditions.
claims.quote: This bond, on my theory, is simply inheritance, that cause which alone, as far as we positively know, produces organisms quite like, or, as we see in the case of varieties nearly like each other.
claims.scope: all organisms within a geographic area, living and fossil
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic clustering of species by region
relatedness of fossil and living species from the same region
claims.candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) combined with fossil occurrences from the Paleobiology Database can test whether regional biotas form clades and whether fossil forms of a region are related to its living forms.

claims.section: Affinity of the productions of the same continent
claims.label: Migration or isolation alone does not cause modification
claims.claim: Migration and isolation do not by themselves cause modification; a group of competing species that migrates together into a new, isolated country will be little modified, because modification is driven by organisms being brought into new relations with one another.
claims.quote: If, for instance, a number of species, which stand in direct competition with each other, migrate in a body into a new and afterwards isolated country, they will be little liable to modification; for neither migration nor isolation in themselves can do anything.
claims.scope: species colonising new isolated areas
measurable_quantities: degree of phenotypic or taxonomic divergence after colonisation
change in the community of competitors experienced by colonists
claims.candidate_data: Comparative studies of island and introduced populations, and experimental-evolution datasets (e.g. on Dryad) that manipulate community composition, could bear on it.

claims.section: Centres of creation
claims.label: Many genera are confined to one region and the most natural genera are local
claims.claim: Some families, many sub-families, very many genera and still more sections of genera are confined to a single region, and the most natural genera (those whose species are most closely related) are generally confined to one area.
claims.quote: Some few families, many sub-families, very many genera, and a still greater number of sections of genera are confined to a single region; and it has been observed by several naturalists, that the most natural genera, or those genera in which the species are most closely related to each other, are generally local, or confined to one area.
claims.scope: higher taxa (families, genera, sections) of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: proportion of taxa endemic to one region at each taxonomic rank
geographic range size of a genus versus the phylogenetic age or tightness of its species
claims.candidate_data: GBIF distributions linked to taxonomic backbones and dated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) allow measuring regional endemism by rank and its relation to clade age.

claims.section: Centres of creation
claims.label: Each species arose in a single area and spread from there
claims.claim: Each species was first produced in one area only and subsequently migrated from that area as far as its powers of migration and subsistence allowed under past and present conditions, rather than arising independently at several points.
claims.quote: Hence it seems to me, as it has to many other naturalists, that the view of each species having been produced in one area alone, and having subsequently migrated from that area as far as its powers of migration and subsistence under past and present conditions permitted, is the most probable.
claims.scope: all species
measurable_quantities: monophyly of conspecific populations across disjunct ranges
geographic origin inferred from phylogeographic structure
claims.candidate_data: Phylogeographic sequence data in GenBank and population-genetic datasets on Dryad allow testing whether disjunct populations of a species share a single geographic origin.

claims.section: Means of dispersal, by changes of climate and of the level of the land, and by occasional means
claims.label: Continents and oceanic islands were not united by land in the recent period
claims.claim: Although continents have undergone great oscillations of level, separate continents have not been continuously joined to each other and to the existing oceanic islands within the period of existing species, contrary to the land-bridge hypotheses of Forbes and others.
claims.quote: But I do not believe that it will ever be proved that within the recent period continents which are now quite separate, have been continuously, or almost continuously, united with each other, and with the many existing oceanic islands.
claims.scope: continents and oceanic islands during the period of existing species
measurable_quantities: bathymetric depth between islands and continents
geological age and origin (volcanic versus continental) of oceanic islands
past land connections reconstructed from sea-level history
claims.candidate_data: GEBCO bathymetry, radiometric ages of oceanic islands from the geological literature, and plate-reconstruction and sea-level records bear directly on it.

claims.section: Means of dispersal, by changes of climate and of the level of the land, and by occasional means
claims.label: About a tenth of a flora's seeds could survive sea-drift across 900 miles
claims.claim: Based on flotation and germination experiments, the seeds of roughly 10 per cent of the plants of a flora, after drying, could be floated by sea currents across about 900 miles of sea and still germinate.
claims.quote: Therefore it would perhaps be safer to assume that the seeds of about 10/100 plants of a flora, after having been dried, could be floated across a space of sea 900 miles in width, and would then germinate.
claims.scope: seeds and fruits of flowering plants exposed to sea-water
measurable_quantities: proportion of species whose diaspores float for a given duration
germination after sea-water immersion
ocean current speeds
claims.candidate_data: Seed-buoyancy trait records (e.g. in the LEDA Traitbase) and published sea-water immersion experiments, combined with ocean-current data, could test the estimate.

claims.section: Means of dispersal, by changes of climate and of the level of the land, and by occasional means
claims.label: Occasional transport bridges hundreds of miles but not distant continents
claims.claim: Occasional means of transport (sea currents, birds, drift timber, icebergs) suffice to carry organisms across a few hundred miles of sea, between islands or from a continent to a nearby island, but not between distant continents, so the floras of distant continents remain distinct.
claims.quote: These means, however, would suffice for occasional transport across tracts of sea some hundred miles in breadth, or from island to island, or from a continent to a neighbouring island, but not from one distant continent to another.
claims.scope: plants (and by extension other organisms) dispersing across seas
measurable_quantities: frequency of long-distance dispersal events by distance
shared species between land masses as a function of separation distance
claims.candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree) used to infer oceanic dispersal events, and island floras in GIFT (Global Inventory of Floras and Traits) against distance to source, could test it.

claims.section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
claims.label: Identical alpine species on distant mountains are relicts of the Glacial period
claims.claim: The same arctic and alpine species on widely separated mountain summits and in arctic regions are relicts of populations that spread across the intervening lowlands during the Glacial period and were stranded on mountains and in the far north as the climate warmed.
claims.quote: Hence, when the warmth had fully returned, the same arctic species, which had lately lived in a body together on the lowlands of the Old and New Worlds, would be left isolated on distant mountain-summits (having been exterminated on all lesser heights) and in the arctic regions of both hemispheres.
claims.scope: arctic-alpine plants and animals of Europe and North America
measurable_quantities: phylogeographic divergence times among mountain populations
fossil and pollen records of arctic species in now-temperate lowlands during glacials
claims.candidate_data: Neotoma Paleoecology Database pollen and macrofossil records together with phylogeographic sequence data in GenBank for arctic-alpine species.

claims.section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
claims.label: North American and European temperate biotas share ancestry from Pliocene circumpolar land
claims.claim: The relationship, with very little identity, between the temperate inhabitants of North America and Europe arises because a common biota inhabited the nearly continuous circumpolar land in warmer Pliocene times and then migrated southward, becoming separated and modified on each continent.
claims.quote: On this view we can understand the relationship, with very little identity, between the productions of North America and Europe,—a relationship which is most remarkable, considering the distance of the two areas, and their separation by the Atlantic Ocean.
claims.scope: temperate plants and animals of North America and Europe
measurable_quantities: divergence times of intercontinental sister taxa
fossil occurrences of shared taxa at high northern latitudes in the Pliocene and earlier Tertiary
claims.candidate_data: Dated phylogenies from TimeTree and fossil occurrences from the Paleobiology Database can test the timing and high-latitude route of North American–European disjunctions.

claims.section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
claims.label: The Glacial period was simultaneous across the whole world
claims.claim: The Glacial period, which lasted a very long time at each place, was at least in part simultaneous across the whole world, or at least along broad longitudinal belts from pole to pole, so that global temperature was lower at the same time.
claims.quote: If this be admitted, it is difficult to avoid believing that the temperature of the whole world was at this period simultaneously cooler.
claims.scope: global climate during the most recent glacial period
measurable_quantities: timing of glacial maxima in both hemispheres
paleotemperature records from tropical and polar regions
claims.candidate_data: Ice-core records (e.g. EPICA Dome C), the LR04 benthic oxygen-isotope stack, and NOAA paleoclimate archives document the timing of glacial cooling worldwide.

claims.section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
claims.label: Plants of high mountains and temperate lowlands worldwide are identical or closely related
claims.claim: Throughout the world, plants growing on high mountains (including tropical ones) and on the temperate lowlands of the northern and southern hemispheres are sometimes identical species but much more often distinct yet closely related species.
claims.quote: Hence we see that throughout the world, the plants growing on the more lofty mountains, and on the temperate lowlands of the northern and southern hemispheres, are sometimes identically the same; but they are much oftener specifically distinct, though related to each other in a most remarkable manner.
claims.scope: flowering plants of temperate lowlands and tropical and temperate mountains
measurable_quantities: number of species and genera shared between northern temperate, tropical montane and southern temperate floras
phylogenetic relatedness of these floras
claims.candidate_data: Plant occurrence and floristic data from GBIF, BIEN and GIFT combined with plant phylogenies from Open Tree of Life.

claims.section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
claims.label: Glacial interchange ran mainly north to south because northern forms were more dominant
claims.claim: Many more identical and allied plant forms migrated from north to south during the Glacial period than in the reverse direction, because the greater land area of the north and the larger populations there had made northern forms more advanced and dominant through natural selection and competition.
claims.quote: I suspect that this preponderant migration from north to south is due to the greater extent of land in the north, and to the northern forms having existed in their own homes in greater numbers, and having consequently been advanced through natural selection and competition to a higher stage of perfection or dominating power, than the southern forms.
claims.scope: plants migrating between hemispheres during the Glacial period
measurable_quantities: number of north-to-south versus south-to-north dispersal events inferred from phylogenies
land area and population size of source regions
claims.candidate_data: Biogeographic reconstructions on dated plant phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) with GBIF distributions can count the direction of inter-hemispheric dispersal events.

claims.section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
claims.label: Northern species naturalise far more often in the south than the reverse
claims.claim: At the present day many European species have become naturalised and partly displaced the natives in La Plata and to a lesser degree in Australia, whereas extremely few southern-hemisphere species have become naturalised anywhere in Europe.
claims.quote: Just in the same manner as we see at the present day, that very many European productions cover the ground in La Plata, and in a lesser degree in Australia, and have to a certain extent beaten the natives; whereas extremely few southern forms have become naturalised in any part of Europe,
claims.scope: naturalised plants and animals exchanged between Europe and southern-hemisphere regions
measurable_quantities: number of species naturalised from Europe in South America and Australia
number of species naturalised from southern regions in Europe
claims.candidate_data: The Global Naturalized Alien Flora (GloNAF) database and DAISIE European alien-species inventories record donor and recipient regions of naturalised species.

claims.section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
claims.label: Distinct southern genera spread from a once-vegetated Antarctica before the Glacial period
claims.claim: Distinct species of genera confined to the southern hemisphere spread in radiating lines from the antarctic lands, which supported a peculiar flora during a warmer period before the Glacial period, reaching southern America, Australia and New Zealand by occasional transport and former islands.
claims.quote: I am inclined to look in the southern, as in the northern hemisphere, to a former and warmer period, before the commencement of the Glacial period, when the antarctic lands, now covered with ice, supported a highly peculiar and isolated flora.
claims.scope: southern-hemisphere plant genera with disjunct distributions
measurable_quantities: fossil plant occurrences in Antarctica
divergence times and inferred ancestral areas of southern disjunct clades
claims.candidate_data: Antarctic fossil plant occurrences in the Paleobiology Database and dated phylogenies of southern clades (e.g. via TimeTree) bear on it.

claims.section: Distribution of fresh-water productions
claims.label: Fresh-water species range widely and allied species occur worldwide
claims.claim: Despite being separated by land and sea barriers, many fresh-water species of quite different classes have enormous ranges, and allied fresh-water species prevail throughout the world.
claims.quote: Not only have many fresh-water species, belonging to quite different classes, an enormous range, but allied species prevail in a remarkable manner throughout the world.
claims.scope: fresh-water plants and animals (insects, molluscs, plants, etc.)
measurable_quantities: geographic range size of fresh-water versus terrestrial species in the same groups
number of continents occupied by fresh-water genera
claims.candidate_data: GBIF occurrence records and freshwater-specific compilations (e.g. Freshwater Ecoregions of the World, IUCN Red List freshwater assessments) can compare range sizes of aquatic and terrestrial taxa.

claims.section: Distribution of fresh-water productions
claims.label: Fresh-water fish species are not shared between distant continents
claims.claim: The same species of fresh-water fish never occur in the fresh waters of distant continents, although within a continent fish species often range widely and irregularly, different river systems sharing some species but not others.
claims.quote: In regard to fish, I believe that the same species never occur in the fresh waters of distant continents. But on the same continent the species often range widely and almost capriciously; for two river-systems will have some fish in common and some different.
claims.scope: fresh-water fishes
measurable_quantities: number of strictly fresh-water fish species native to more than one continent
species overlap between river basins within a continent
claims.candidate_data: FishBase distribution records and global freshwater fish occurrence-by-drainage-basin compilations, together with GBIF, can test both parts.

claims.section: Distribution of fresh-water productions
claims.label: Water birds disperse seeds and eggs, explaining wide ranges of fresh-water life
claims.claim: The wide distribution of fresh-water plants and lower fresh-water animals depends mainly on the transport of their seeds and eggs by animals, especially wide-flying fresh-water birds that move between often distant bodies of water.
claims.quote: But the wide distribution of fresh-water plants and of the lower animals, whether retaining the same identical form or in some degree modified, I believe mainly depends on the wide dispersal of their seeds and eggs by animals, more especially by fresh-water birds, which have large powers of flight, and naturally travel from one to another and often distant piece of water.
claims.scope: fresh-water plants and small fresh-water invertebrates
measurable_quantities: frequency of viable propagules carried externally or internally by waterbirds
waterbird movement distances
genetic connectivity of aquatic populations along flyways
claims.candidate_data: Waterbird tracking data in Movebank and published waterbird propagule-transport studies, with population-genetic data in GenBank or Dryad for aquatic plants and invertebrates.

claims.section: On the inhabitants of oceanic islands
claims.label: Oceanic islands have fewer species than equal continental areas
claims.claim: Oceanic islands are inhabited by far fewer species of all kinds than continental areas of equal size, a difference not explained by physical conditions.
claims.quote: The species of all kinds which inhabit oceanic islands are few in number compared with those on equal continental areas
claims.scope: plants and animals of oceanic islands compared with continental areas
measurable_quantities: native species richness per unit area on oceanic islands versus continental samples of equal area
claims.candidate_data: Island and mainland checklists in GIFT (Global Inventory of Floras and Traits) and GBIF allow species-area comparisons between oceanic islands and continental regions.

claims.section: On the inhabitants of oceanic islands
claims.label: Oceanic islands have a very high proportion of endemic species
claims.claim: Although oceanic islands have few species, the proportion of their species that are endemic (found nowhere else) is often extremely large relative to their area, as expected if occasional colonists arriving in a new isolated district are especially liable to modification.
claims.quote: Although in oceanic islands the number of kinds of inhabitants is scanty, the proportion of endemic species (_i.e._ those found nowhere else in the world) is often extremely large.
claims.scope: plants and animals of oceanic islands
measurable_quantities: proportion of endemic species on oceanic islands
endemic species per unit area on islands versus continents
claims.candidate_data: GIFT island floras with endemism status, IUCN Red List and BirdLife range data for vertebrates, and GBIF occurrences.

claims.section: On the inhabitants of oceanic islands
claims.label: Island endemism is low in groups that arrive easily and in numbers
claims.claim: Within one island, some groups are almost wholly endemic while others are not, because groups that immigrate readily and in a body (e.g. marine birds, sea-shells, regularly visiting land-birds) keep their mutual relations undisturbed and so are little modified.
claims.quote: But it by no means follows, that, because in an island nearly all the species of one class are peculiar, those of another class, or of another section of the same class, are peculiar; and this difference seems to depend on the species which do not become modified having immigrated with facility and in a body, so that their mutual relations have not been much disturbed.
claims.scope: groups of organisms on oceanic islands differing in dispersal ability
measurable_quantities: proportion of endemic species per taxonomic group on an island
dispersal ability or immigration frequency of each group
claims.candidate_data: Island checklists with endemism status (GIFT, BirdLife, IUCN Red List) combined with dispersal traits (e.g. AVONET hand-wing index for birds) allow testing whether endemism declines with dispersal ability.

claims.section: On the inhabitants of oceanic islands
claims.label: Natural selection turns island herbaceous plants into shrubs and trees
claims.claim: Because trees rarely reach distant oceanic islands, herbaceous plants that colonise them gain an advantage by growing taller, so natural selection often converts insular herbaceous plants first into bushes and then into trees, explaining why islands have trees in orders that are elsewhere herbaceous.
claims.quote: If so, natural selection would often tend to add to the stature of herbaceous plants when growing on an island, to whatever order they belonged, and thus convert them first into bushes and ultimately into trees.
claims.scope: flowering plants on oceanic islands
measurable_quantities: frequency of derived woodiness in island versus mainland lineages
phylogenetic transitions from herbaceous to woody growth form
claims.candidate_data: Global compilations of derived insular woodiness from the botanical literature, combined with plant phylogenies (Open Tree of Life) and growth-form data in the TRY plant trait database.

claims.section: Absence of Batrachians and of terrestrial Mammals
claims.label: Frogs, toads and newts are absent from oceanic islands
claims.claim: Batrachians (frogs, toads and newts) are naturally absent from oceanic islands, not because conditions there are unsuitable (introduced frogs thrive) but because they and their spawn are killed by sea-water and so cannot cross the sea.
claims.quote: Bory St. Vincent long ago remarked that Batrachians (frogs, toads, newts) have never been found on any of the many islands with which the great oceans are studded. I have taken pains to verify this assertion, and I have found it strictly true.
claims.scope: amphibians on oceanic islands
measurable_quantities: presence of native amphibian species on oceanic islands
establishment success of introduced amphibians on oceanic islands
claims.candidate_data: AmphibiaWeb and IUCN Red List amphibian range maps, plus GBIF records and island geological origin, can test native amphibian occurrence on oceanic islands.

claims.section: Absence of Batrachians and of terrestrial Mammals
claims.label: No native terrestrial mammals on islands more than 300 miles from a continent
claims.claim: No native terrestrial mammal inhabits any island more than about 300 miles from a continent or large continental island, even though small mammals thrive when introduced there, because terrestrial mammals cannot cross wide stretches of sea.
claims.quote: as yet I have not found a single instance, free from doubt, of a terrestrial mammal (excluding domesticated animals kept by the natives) inhabiting an island situated above 300 miles from a continent or great continental island;
claims.scope: native non-flying mammals on islands
measurable_quantities: presence of native terrestrial mammals by island isolation distance
establishment of introduced mammals on remote islands
claims.candidate_data: Native mammal ranges from PHYLACINE or IUCN Red List range maps, overlaid with island locations and distance to mainland.

claims.section: Absence of Batrachians and of terrestrial Mammals
claims.label: Bats occur on almost every island, often as endemic species
claims.claim: Although terrestrial mammals are absent from oceanic islands, bats occur on almost every island, and remote islands often have their own endemic bat species, because bats can fly across wide spaces of sea and are then modified in their new homes.
claims.quote: Though terrestrial mammals do not occur on oceanic islands, ærial mammals do occur on almost every island.
claims.scope: bats on oceanic islands
measurable_quantities: presence and number of native bat species on oceanic islands
proportion of island bat species that are endemic
claims.candidate_data: IUCN Red List and PHYLACINE bat range data combined with island geography, and GBIF occurrence records.

claims.section: Absence of Batrachians and of terrestrial Mammals
claims.label: Sea depth between island and mainland predicts their mammalian affinity
claims.claim: Somewhat independently of distance, the depth of sea separating an island from the neighbouring mainland is related to whether they share the same or allied mammal species: islands separated by shallow channels have the same or very similar mammals, those across deep water have distinct species and genera.
claims.quote: there is also a relation, to a certain extent independent of distance, between the depth of the sea separating an island from the neighbouring mainland, and the presence in both of the same mammiferous species or of allied species in a more or less modified condition.
claims.scope: terrestrial mammals of continental and near-continental islands
measurable_quantities: depth of the channel between island and mainland
proportion of island mammal species shared with or congeneric with the mainland
island–mainland distance
claims.candidate_data: GEBCO bathymetry combined with mammal ranges from PHYLACINE or IUCN Red List and a mammal phylogeny (e.g. via Open Tree of Life).

claims.section: On the relation of the inhabitants of islands to those of the nearest mainland
claims.label: Island endemics are related to species of the nearest continent
claims.claim: It is an almost universal rule that the endemic species of islands are related to those of the nearest continent or other nearby islands, even when the islands' physical conditions resemble those of a different, more distant region (e.g. Galapagos to America, Cape Verde to Africa).
claims.quote: indeed it is an almost universal rule that the endemic productions of islands are related to those of the nearest continent, or of other near islands.
claims.scope: endemic plants and animals of oceanic islands
measurable_quantities: geographic location of the closest relatives (sister lineages) of island endemics
distance from island to the source region versus to the nearest continent
claims.candidate_data: Phylogenies in Open Tree of Life and sequence data in GenBank, combined with GBIF distributions, allow identifying the source region of island endemic lineages.

claims.section: On the relation of the inhabitants of islands to those of the nearest mainland
claims.label: Species on islands of one archipelago are closest relatives of each other
claims.claim: The distinct species inhabiting the separate islands of an archipelago are far more closely related to one another than to the inhabitants of any other part of the world, because the islands received immigrants from the same source or from each other.
claims.quote: so that the inhabitants of each separate island, though mostly distinct, are related in an incomparably closer degree to each other than to the inhabitants of any other part of the world.
claims.scope: endemic species of oceanic archipelagos
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic relatedness among species on different islands of an archipelago versus to mainland species
claims.candidate_data: Molecular phylogenies of archipelago radiations from GenBank and Open Tree of Life (e.g. Galapagos finches and mockingbirds).

claims.section: On the relation of the inhabitants of islands to those of the nearest mainland
claims.label: Naturalised species are usually not closely allied to the natives they join
claims.claim: Species that become naturalised in new countries are generally not closely allied to the native inhabitants but are very distinct, often belonging to genera absent from the region, whereas closely allied species equally well fitted to their places tend to keep separate.
claims.quote: the forms which become naturalised in new countries are not generally closely allied to the aboriginal inhabitants, but are very distinct species, belonging in a large proportion of cases, as shown by Alph. de Candolle, to distinct genera.
claims.scope: naturalised (introduced) plants and animals
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distance between naturalised species and the native flora or fauna
proportion of naturalised species belonging to genera not native to the region
claims.candidate_data: GloNAF naturalised-plant records combined with regional native floras (GIFT) and plant phylogenies (Open Tree of Life) allow direct tests.

claims.section: On colonisation from the nearest source with subsequent modification
claims.label: Inhabitants of any area are modified colonists from the most accessible source
claims.claim: The inhabitants of any area (oceanic islands, mountains, lakes, marshes, caves), where not identical, are plainly related to those of the region from which colonists could most readily have come, the colonists having since been modified and better fitted to their new homes.
claims.quote: The principle which determines the general character of the fauna and flora of oceanic islands, namely, that the inhabitants, when not identically the same, yet are plainly related to the inhabitants of that region whence colonists could most readily have been derived,—the colonists having been subsequently modified and better fitted to their new homes,—is of the widest application throughout nature.
claims.scope: biotas of islands, mountains, lakes, marshes and caves
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic relatedness of alpine, cave or lake species to species of surrounding lowlands versus distant similar habitats
claims.candidate_data: Phylogenies from Open Tree of Life and GenBank sequences for alpine, cave and lake lineages, combined with GBIF distributions of their relatives.

claims.section: On colonisation from the nearest source with subsequent modification
claims.label: Regions sharing many allied species will also share some identical species
claims.claim: Wherever two regions, however distant, contain many closely allied or representative species, they will also contain some identical species and many doubtful forms ranked variously as species or varieties, showing past migration between them.
claims.quote: And it will, I believe, be universally found to be true, that wherever in two regions, let them be ever so distant, many closely allied or representative species occur, there will likewise be found some identical species
claims.scope: pairs of geographic regions with related biotas
measurable_quantities: number of allied (congeneric) species shared between two regions
number of identical species shared between the same regions
claims.candidate_data: GBIF occurrences or regional checklists (e.g. GIFT for plants) can measure the correlation between shared congeners and shared species across region pairs.

claims.section: On colonisation from the nearest source with subsequent modification
claims.label: The lower a group of organisms, the more widely it tends to range
claims.claim: Organisms lower in the scale of nature tend to range more widely than higher ones, because they change more slowly and their seeds and eggs are minute and suited to distant transport.
claims.quote: namely, that the lower any group of organisms is, the more widely it is apt to range.
claims.scope: plants and animals across taxonomic groups considered 'lower' and 'higher'
measurable_quantities: geographic range size of species or genera by group
rate of morphological change by group
propagule size
claims.candidate_data: GBIF occurrence-derived range sizes across major groups, with Paleobiology Database species durations as a proxy for rate of change.

claims.section: Summary
claims.label: Closer relatives tend to be closer together in time and space
claims.claim: Because forms within each class are connected by ordinary generation, the more closely two forms are related by descent, the nearer they will generally be to each other in time and in geographic space.
claims.quote: and the more nearly any two forms are related in blood, the nearer they will generally stand to each other in time and space;
claims.scope: all organisms, living and fossil
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distance between species pairs
geographic distance between their ranges
stratigraphic separation between fossil taxa
claims.candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) combined with GBIF range data and Paleobiology Database occurrences allow testing the correlation of phylogenetic with geographic and temporal distance.

claims.section: CLASSIFICATION, groups subordinate to groups
claims.label: Descent with divergence and extinction produces groups subordinate to groups
claims.claim: The nested arrangement of organisms into groups within groups (species within genera, genera within families, and so on) results from the modified descendants of a single progenitor diverging in character while less divergent forms are exterminated.
claims.quote: he will see that the inevitable result is that the modified descendants proceeding from one progenitor become broken up into groups subordinate to groups.
claims.scope: all organic beings, living and extinct
measurable_quantities: degree of hierarchical (tree-like) structure in character or sequence data
consistency of nested clades across independent character sets
claims.candidate_data: Large phylogenies and their underlying character and sequence matrices (Open Tree of Life, GenBank, TreeBASE) allow tests of how tree-like the pattern of similarity is.

claims.section: Natural system
claims.label: The Natural System expresses propinquity of descent
claims.claim: The 'something more' than mere resemblance that naturalists seek in the Natural System is closeness of descent, which is the only known cause of similarity among organisms and is partially revealed by classifications.
claims.quote: propinquity of descent,—the only known cause of the similarity of organic beings,—is the bond, hidden as it is by various degrees of modification, which is partially revealed to us by our classifications.
claims.scope: biological classification of all organisms
measurable_quantities: congruence between traditional morphology-based classifications and independently inferred phylogenies
claims.candidate_data: Comparison of traditional Linnaean taxonomies (e.g. Catalogue of Life, GBIF backbone) with phylogenies from Open Tree of Life.

claims.section: Rules and difficulties in classification, explained on the theory of descent with modification
claims.label: Characters least modified by adaptation are most constant and useful in classification
claims.claim: The value of a character for classification depends on its constancy across large groups of species, and characters are constant when they have been little changed in adapting species to their conditions of life; hence parts least concerned with special habits are generally the most useful for classification.
claims.quote: But their importance for classification, I believe, depends on their greater constancy throughout large groups of species; and this constancy depends on such organs having generally been subjected to less change in the adaptation of the species to their conditions of life.
claims.scope: characters of animals and plants used in systematics
measurable_quantities: homoplasy or consistency index of characters
association between a character's ecological/functional relevance and its homoplasy
claims.candidate_data: Published morphological character matrices (MorphoBank, TreeBASE) analysed on reference phylogenies to compare homoplasy of habit-related versus other characters.

claims.section: Rules and difficulties in classification, explained on the theory of descent with modification
claims.label: Higher taxonomic ranks are almost arbitrary
claims.claim: The relative value of groups such as orders, sub-orders, families, sub-families and genera is, at least at present, almost arbitrary, as shown by groups being raised in rank merely because more allied species were discovered.
claims.quote: Finally, with respect to the comparative value of the various groups of species, such as orders, sub-orders, families, sub-families, and genera, they seem to be, at least at present, almost arbitrary.
claims.scope: taxonomic ranks above the species level
measurable_quantities: variation in crown or stem age of taxa of the same rank
variation in species richness and disparity among taxa of the same rank
claims.candidate_data: Divergence times of genera, families and orders across groups from TimeTree, with taxonomy from the Catalogue of Life or GBIF backbone.

claims.section: Rules and difficulties in classification, explained on the theory of descent with modification
claims.label: Branches equally related by descent can differ greatly in amount of modification
claims.claim: A natural arrangement of groups must be strictly genealogical, but branches that are equally closely related to a common progenitor may differ greatly in how much they have been modified, and these differing amounts of difference are what is expressed by ranking them as different genera, families or orders.
claims.quote: I believe that the _arrangement_ of the groups within each class, in due subordination and relation to the other groups, must be strictly genealogical in order to be natural; but that the _amount_ of difference in the several branches or groups, though allied in the same degree in blood to their common progenitor, may differ greatly, being due to the different degrees of modification which they have undergone
claims.scope: all classes of organisms
measurable_quantities: morphological disparity or rate of change among sister lineages of equal age
variation in evolutionary rates among lineages
claims.candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) combined with morphological matrices (MorphoBank) to compare rates of morphological change across sister clades.

claims.section: Classification of varieties
claims.label: Varieties form nested groups for the same reason species do
claims.claim: Domestic and natural varieties fall into groups subordinate to groups (sub-varieties under varieties under species) for the same reason species do, namely closeness of descent combined with various degrees of modification.
claims.quote: The origin of the existence of groups subordinate to groups, is the same with varieties as with species, namely, closeness of descent with various degrees of modification.
claims.scope: varieties and breeds of domestic and wild species
measurable_quantities: hierarchical clustering of breeds or varieties
agreement between breed clustering and documented breed histories
claims.candidate_data: Genome-wide population data for domestic breeds (e.g. dog, pigeon, cattle and chicken breed panels in GenBank/SRA) compared with recorded breed pedigrees.

claims.section: Descent always used in classification
claims.label: Characters shared across species with very different habits indicate common inheritance
claims.claim: However trifling a character, if it occurs throughout many species with very different habits of life it can be explained only by inheritance from a common parent, and so has high value for classification; for the same reason rudimentary structures can be as useful as other parts.
claims.quote: if it prevail throughout many and different species, especially those having very different habits of life, it assumes high value; for we can account for its presence in so many forms with such different habits, only by its inheritance from a common parent.
claims.scope: characters of animals and plants within large groups
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic signal of characters
fit of character distributions to a single origin versus multiple origins
claims.candidate_data: Trait datasets mapped onto phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, TreeBASE, MorphoBank) to estimate the number of origins of widely shared characters.

claims.section: Analogical or adaptive characters
claims.label: Distinct lineages adapted to similar conditions converge in external form
claims.claim: Animals from very distinct lines of descent can become adapted to similar conditions and so acquire a close external resemblance; such analogical or adaptive resemblances conceal rather than reveal blood-relationship, so they are almost worthless for classification between groups, although the same characters can indicate true affinity within a group.
claims.quote: For animals, belonging to two most distinct lines of descent, may readily become adapted to similar conditions, and thus assume a close external resemblance; but such resemblances will not reveal—will rather tend to conceal their blood-relationship to their proper lines of descent.
claims.scope: animals (and plants) of distinct lineages living under similar conditions
measurable_quantities: frequency of convergent morphological evolution
mismatch between morphology-based groupings and phylogeny for habit-related traits
claims.candidate_data: Phylogenies from Open Tree of Life combined with ecomorphological trait data (e.g. AVONET for birds, PanTHERIA for mammals) to quantify convergence among unrelated lineages.

claims.section: CLASSIFICATION, groups subordinate to groups
claims.label: Expanding dominant groups explain why all life falls into a few great classes
claims.claim: Larger and more dominant groups tend to keep increasing in size and to supplant smaller, feebler groups, which is why all organisms, recent and extinct, fall into a few great orders, still fewer classes, and a single natural system.
claims.quote: The larger and more dominant groups thus tend to go on increasing in size; and they consequently supplant many smaller and feebler groups. Thus we can account for the fact that all organisms, recent and extinct, are included under a few great orders, under still fewer classes, and all in one great natural system.
claims.scope: all higher taxa through geological time
measurable_quantities: relationship between clade size and subsequent diversification rate
clade extinction rate as a function of clade size
claims.candidate_data: Fossil occurrence data from the Paleobiology Database and dated molecular phylogenies (TimeTree) to test whether large clades grow and small clades disappear.

claims.section: Affinities, general, complex and radiating
claims.label: Aberrant groups are species-poor relicts of extinction
claims.claim: Aberrant or osculant groups are the surviving remnants of failing groups that suffered heavy extinction; consequently they are generally represented by very few species, and those species are usually very distinct from each other.
claims.quote: And we have some evidence of aberrant forms having suffered severely from extinction, for they are generally represented by extremely few species; and such species as do occur are generally very distinct from each other, which again implies extinction.
claims.scope: aberrant (phylogenetically isolated) genera and higher groups
measurable_quantities: species richness of phylogenetically isolated lineages
branch length or evolutionary distinctiveness
fossil diversity history of relict clades
claims.candidate_data: Evolutionary-distinctiveness scores computed on large phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree) compared with clade species richness, plus Paleobiology Database records of past diversity of relict clades.

claims.section: Affinities, general, complex and radiating
claims.label: Affinities of one group to another are usually general, not to any single species
claims.claim: When a member of one group shows a real affinity to a quite distinct group, the affinity is usually general rather than to any particular species, because it retains characters of an ancient common progenitor of both groups.
claims.quote: when a member belonging to one group of animals exhibits an affinity to a quite distinct group, this affinity in most cases is general and not special
claims.scope: members of distinct orders or families of animals and plants that show cross-group affinities
measurable_quantities: similarity of a taxon to each member of another group
phylogenetic position of taxa showing cross-group affinity (near the base of their group or not)
claims.candidate_data: Morphological matrices (MorphoBank) and phylogenies (Open Tree of Life) to test whether taxa with cross-group affinities are early-diverging lineages.

claims.section: Extinction separates and defines groups
claims.label: Gaps between groups, even whole classes, are due to extinction of connecting forms
claims.claim: Extinction has defined and widened the intervals between groups; even the distinctness of whole classes, such as birds from other vertebrates, results from the loss of many ancient forms that once connected their early progenitors.
claims.quote: We may thus account even for the distinctness of whole classes from each other—for instance, of birds from all other vertebrate animals—by the belief that many ancient forms of life have been utterly lost, through which the early progenitors of birds were formerly connected with the early progenitors of the other vertebrate classes.
claims.scope: classes and other higher groups, especially vertebrate classes
measurable_quantities: occurrence of fossil forms intermediate between currently distinct classes
morphological gap between groups before and after including fossil taxa
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrences and published fossil character matrices (MorphoBank), e.g. for the dinosaur-to-bird transition.

claims.section: MORPHOLOGY, between members of the same class, between parts of the same individual
claims.label: Homologous parts change shape and size but keep the same relative connexions
claims.claim: Within a class, homologous parts may change to almost any extent in form and size but always remain connected in the same order; for example, the bones of the arm and forearm are never transposed.
claims.quote: the parts may change to almost any extent in form and size, and yet they always remain connected together in the same order.
claims.scope: homologous structures within classes (vertebrate limbs, insect mouthparts, crustacean limbs, flowers)
measurable_quantities: frequency of changes in topological connectivity of homologous elements versus changes in shape and size
claims.candidate_data: Comparative anatomical datasets and ontologies (e.g. Uberon, MorphoBank matrices) recording element connectivity across taxa.

claims.section: MORPHOLOGY, between members of the same class, between parts of the same individual
claims.label: Unity of type reflects a common progenitor's pattern modified by slight steps
claims.claim: The shared pattern of homologous organs within a class is explained by descent from an ancient progenitor (an archetype) that already had that pattern, which natural selection then modified by slight successive steps for different uses without transposing parts.
claims.quote: If we suppose that the ancient progenitor, the archetype as it may be called, of all mammals, had its limbs constructed on the existing general pattern, for whatever purpose they served, we can at once perceive the plain signification of the homologous construction of the limbs throughout the whole class.
claims.scope: members of the same class (e.g. mammal limbs, insect mouthparts)
measurable_quantities: presence of the shared pattern in early fossil members of the class
reconstructed ancestral states of homologous structures
claims.candidate_data: Fossil occurrence and morphology data (Paleobiology Database, MorphoBank) for early members of classes, with ancestral-state reconstruction on Open Tree of Life phylogenies.

claims.section: MORPHOLOGY, between members of the same class, between parts of the same individual
claims.label: Serially homologous parts derive from many repeated similar elements in progenitors
claims.claim: Serial homologies within one individual (skull and vertebrae, jaws and legs of crustaceans, floral parts and leaves) arise because the progenitors of vertebrates, articulates and flowering plants had many repeated similar parts, which natural selection adapted to diverse purposes while inheritance retained a fundamental resemblance.
claims.quote: An indefinite repetition of the same part or organ is the common characteristic (as Owen has observed) of all low or little-modified forms; therefore we may readily believe that the unknown progenitor of the vertebrata possessed many vertebræ; the unknown progenitor of the articulata, many segments; and the unknown progenitor of flowering plants, many spiral whorls of leaves.
claims.scope: vertebrates, articulates (arthropods and annelids) and flowering plants
measurable_quantities: number and similarity of serially repeated elements in early fossil members versus later members of each group
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrences and fossil morphological matrices (MorphoBank) for early arthropods, vertebrates and seed plants.

claims.section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
claims.label: Embryos of different animals in the same class are strikingly similar
claims.claim: Embryos of distinct animals within the same class are often strikingly similar, more so than the adults, and the points of resemblance often have no direct relation to their conditions of existence.
claims.quote: The embryos, also, of distinct animals within the same class are often strikingly similar
claims.scope: animals within the same class, especially vertebrates and insects
measurable_quantities: morphological similarity of embryos across species by developmental stage
embryonic versus adult between-species divergence
claims.candidate_data: Comparative embryo image and staging collections and published cross-species developmental time series (morphological and transcriptomic) for vertebrates and insects.

claims.section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
claims.label: Active larvae are adapted to their own conditions as fully as adults
claims.claim: Whenever an embryo or larva becomes active and must provide for itself, it is as perfectly adapted to its conditions of life as the adult, and such adaptations can make the larvae of allied species differ as much as or more than their adults, though most larvae still follow the law of embryonic resemblance.
claims.quote: The period of activity may come on earlier or later in life; but whenever it comes on, the adaptation of the larva to its conditions of life is just as perfect and as beautiful as in the adult animal.
claims.scope: animals with free-living larval stages (e.g. insects, crustaceans, cirripedes)
measurable_quantities: larval versus adult morphological divergence among allied species
association between larval ecology and larval morphology
claims.candidate_data: Comparative larval and adult morphological datasets for marine invertebrates and insects mapped on phylogenies from Open Tree of Life.

claims.section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
claims.label: Young of domestic breeds differ much less than adults
claims.claim: The characteristic differences between domestic breeds produced by man's selection (in dogs, horses and pigeons) generally do not appear early in life and are inherited at a corresponding later age, so that the young of different breeds differ far less in proportions than the adults, with occasional exceptions such as the short-faced tumbler pigeon.
claims.quote: the characteristic differences which give value to each breed, and which have been accumulated by man’s selection, have not generally first appeared at an early period of life, and have been inherited by the offspring at a corresponding not early period.
claims.scope: domestic breeds of dogs, horses and pigeons
measurable_quantities: proportional differences between breeds at hatching or birth versus adulthood
ontogenetic allometric trajectories by breed
claims.candidate_data: Published ontogenetic morphometric data for dog and pigeon breeds (e.g. skull growth series in museum collections and Dryad datasets).

claims.section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
claims.label: Community of embryonic structure reveals community of descent
claims.claim: Because the embryo is the animal in a less modified state that partly reveals the structure of its progenitor, two groups that pass through the same or similar embryonic stages are descended from the same or similar parents, however different their adults; this is why embryonic characters are the most valuable for classification.
claims.quote: Thus, community in embryonic structure reveals community of descent.
claims.scope: animal groups, e.g. cirripedes recognised as crustaceans by their larvae
measurable_quantities: agreement between groupings based on embryonic/larval characters and independent phylogenies
agreement between adult-character groupings and independent phylogenies
claims.candidate_data: Larval and adult morphological matrices (MorphoBank) compared against molecular phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, GenBank).

claims.section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
claims.label: Ancient extinct forms should resemble the embryos of their living descendants
claims.claim: Since embryos partly show the structure of less modified ancient progenitors, ancient and extinct forms should resemble the embryos of their living descendants, though this may be obscured by early-appearing variations and may be undemonstrable because the geological record does not reach back far enough.
claims.quote: we can clearly see why ancient and extinct forms of life should resemble the embryos of their descendants,—our existing species.
claims.scope: extinct ancestors and the embryos of their living descendants
measurable_quantities: similarity of fossil adult morphology to embryonic versus adult morphology of living relatives
claims.candidate_data: Fossil morphological data (Paleobiology Database, MorphoBank) combined with ontogenetic series of living relatives.

claims.section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
claims.label: Embryological facts follow from late-appearing variations inherited at corresponding ages
claims.claim: The leading facts of embryology are explained because, in the descendants of a common progenitor, successive slight modifications generally do not appear at a very early period of life (though they may be caused earlier) and are inherited at a corresponding later age, leaving embryos little modified.
claims.quote: the leading facts in embryology, which are second in importance to none in natural history, are explained on the principle of slight modifications not appearing, in the many descendants from some one ancient progenitor, at a very early period in the life of each, though perhaps caused at the earliest, and being inherited at a corresponding not early period.
claims.scope: animals generally
measurable_quantities: developmental stage at which between-species differences first appear
divergence of developmental trajectories across ontogeny
claims.candidate_data: Comparative ontogenetic morphometric series and cross-species developmental time series for vertebrates and insects.

claims.section: RUDIMENTARY ORGANS; their origin explained
claims.label: Rudimentary organs are extremely common throughout nature
claims.claim: Rudimentary, atrophied or aborted organs that bear the stamp of uselessness are extremely common in animals and plants.
claims.quote: Organs or parts in this strange condition, bearing the stamp of inutility, are extremely common throughout nature.
claims.scope: animals and plants generally
measurable_quantities: proportion of taxa possessing vestigial structures
number of documented vestigial structures per clade
claims.candidate_data: Comparative anatomical databases and ontologies (e.g. Uberon, Phenoscape) annotated for reduced or vestigial structures.

claims.section: RUDIMENTARY ORGANS; their origin explained
claims.label: Rudimentary organs are highly variable
claims.claim: Rudimentary organs vary greatly in development among individuals of the same species, and the degree of reduction of the same organ can differ much between closely allied species; because they are useless, their variations are not checked by natural selection.
claims.quote: Rudimentary organs in the individuals of the same species are very liable to vary in degree of development and in other respects.
claims.scope: rudimentary organs in animals and plants
measurable_quantities: within-species coefficient of variation of vestigial versus functional structures
claims.candidate_data: Morphometric data on vestigial structures (e.g. cave-fish eyes, flightless-bird wings) in museum collections and Dryad datasets.

claims.section: RUDIMENTARY ORGANS; their origin explained
claims.label: Rudimentary organs are relatively larger in the embryo than in the adult
claims.claim: As a universal rule, a rudimentary part is relatively larger compared with adjoining parts in the embryo than in the adult, and some rudiments (such as the teeth of whales and ruminants) appear in the embryo and then wholly disappear.
claims.quote: It is also, I believe, a universal rule, that a rudimentary part or organ is of greater size relatively to the adjoining parts in the embryo, than in the adult
claims.scope: rudimentary organs in animals and plants
measurable_quantities: relative size of rudimentary organs across ontogenetic stages
claims.candidate_data: Ontogenetic series and embryological descriptions of vestigial structures (e.g. whale and ruminant tooth germs, snake limb buds) in museum collections and literature.

claims.section: RUDIMENTARY ORGANS; their origin explained
claims.label: Disuse is the main cause of rudimentary organs
claims.claim: Disuse over successive generations has been the main agency reducing organs to rudiments (as with eyes of cave animals and wings of island birds), aided by natural selection where an organ becomes injurious; because reduction occurs at maturity and is inherited at a corresponding age, rudiments remain relatively larger in the embryo.
claims.quote: I believe that disuse has been the main agency; that it has led in successive generations to the gradual reduction of various organs, until they have become rudimentary
claims.scope: organs reduced under changed habits or conditions, e.g. cave animals and island birds
measurable_quantities: degree of organ reduction versus time since habitat change
evidence of reduction under relaxed versus active selection
claims.candidate_data: Studies of cave-fish (Astyanax) and island flightless birds with dated phylogenies (TimeTree), plus experimental-evolution datasets in Dryad.

claims.section: How far the theory of natural selection may be extended
claims.label: Descent with modification embraces all members of each class
claims.claim: Because all members of whole classes are linked by chains of affinities, fossils fill wide gaps between orders, rudiments imply fully developed ancestral organs, and structures within a class share one pattern and similar embryos, descent with modification embraces all members of the same class.
claims.quote: Therefore I cannot doubt that the theory of descent with modification embraces all the members of the same class.
claims.scope: all members of each class of animals and plants
measurable_quantities: monophyly of classes in independent phylogenies
support for common ancestry within each class
claims.candidate_data: Phylogenomic datasets and synthetic trees (Open Tree of Life, GenBank/SRA) testing monophyly and common ancestry of classes.

claims.section: How far the theory of natural selection may be extended
claims.label: Animals from at most four or five progenitors, plants from as many or fewer
claims.claim: All animals have descended from at most four or five progenitors, and all plants from an equal or smaller number.
claims.quote: I believe that animals have descended from at most only four or five progenitors, and plants from an equal or lesser number.
claims.scope: all animals and all plants
measurable_quantities: number of independent origins of animals and of plants inferred from phylogenetic data
claims.candidate_data: Phylogenomic data for animals and plants (GenBank/SRA, Open Tree of Life) testing monophyly of each kingdom versus multiple independent origins.

claims.section: How far the theory of natural selection may be extended
claims.label: All living things share chemical composition, cell structure and laws of growth
claims.claim: All living things have much in common in their chemical composition, germinal vesicles, cellular structure, and laws of growth and reproduction, as shown even by the same poison often affecting plants and animals similarly.
claims.quote: Nevertheless all living things have much in common, in their chemical composition, their germinal vesicles, their cellular structure, and their laws of growth and reproduction.
claims.scope: all living organisms
measurable_quantities: shared biochemical components and pathways across kingdoms
shared cellular structures across kingdoms
claims.candidate_data: Cross-kingdom biochemical pathway and protein databases (KEGG, UniProt) documenting shared metabolism and cell components.

claims.section: How far the theory of natural selection may be extended
claims.label: Probably all organisms descend from one primordial form
claims.claim: By analogy, probably all organisms that have ever lived on earth have descended from a single primordial form.
claims.quote: Therefore I should infer from analogy that probably all the organic beings which have ever lived on this earth have descended from some one primordial form, into which life was first breathed.
claims.scope: all organisms that have ever lived on earth
measurable_quantities: statistical support for universal common ancestry versus multiple independent origins
claims.candidate_data: Universally conserved sequence data (e.g. ribosomal RNA and protein sequences in GenBank, SILVA) used in formal tests of universal common ancestry.

claims.section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
claims.label: Species differ from varieties only in their intermediates having existed formerly
claims.claim: The only distinction between species and well-marked varieties is that varieties are known or believed to be connected by intermediate gradations at present, whereas species were connected by them in the past; species should therefore be treated, like genera, as combinations made for convenience.
claims.quote: Hereafter we shall be compelled to acknowledge that the only distinction between species and well-marked varieties is, that the latter are known, or believed, to be connected at the present day by intermediate gradations, whereas species were formerly thus connected.
claims.scope: species and varieties of all organisms
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
claims.label: Organism-to-organism relations are the most important cause of organic change
claims.claim: The most important cause of organic change is the mutual relation of organism to organism, in which the improvement of one form causes the improvement or extermination of others; this is almost independent of changes, even sudden ones, in physical conditions.
claims.quote: the most important of all causes of organic change is one which is almost independent of altered and perhaps suddenly altered physical conditions, namely, the mutual relation of organism to organism,—the improvement of one being entailing the improvement or the extermination of others
claims.scope: all organisms over geological time
measurable_quantities: relative explanatory power of biotic interactions (diversity, competitors) versus abiotic change (climate, sea level) for origination and extinction rates
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrence data analysed together with paleoclimate and sea-level records.

claims.section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
claims.label: Amount of fossil change between formations measures elapsed time
claims.claim: Because species are produced and exterminated by slow, still-acting causes, the amount of organic change in the fossils of consecutive formations is probably a fair, though imperfect, measure of the time elapsed, and can be used to estimate the length of the blank intervals between formations.
claims.quote: it follows, that the amount of organic change in the fossils of consecutive formations probably serves as a fair measure of the lapse of actual time.
claims.scope: fossil faunas and floras of successive formations
measurable_quantities: faunal turnover between successive units
radiometrically dated time intervals between units
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrences with ages from the Geologic Time Scale to correlate taxonomic turnover with absolute elapsed time.

claims.section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
claims.label: Rate of organic change was slower early in life's history
claims.claim: In early periods of earth's history, when forms of life were fewer and simpler, the rate of organic change was probably slower, and at the first dawn of life it may have been extremely slow.
claims.quote: During early periods of the earth’s history, when the forms of life were probably fewer and simpler, the rate of change was probably slower; and at the first dawn of life, when very few forms of the simplest structure existed, the rate of change may have been slow in an extreme degree.
claims.scope: life on earth across its whole history
measurable_quantities: origination and extinction rates through time
rates of morphological change in early versus later clades
relationship between standing diversity and rate of change
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database diversity and turnover curves through the Phanerozoic, plus Precambrian microfossil and dated-phylogeny data (TimeTree).

claims.section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
claims.label: Known geological history is a fragment of the time since the first organism
claims.claim: The whole history of the world as known from geology is only a small fragment of the time that has elapsed since the first organism, the progenitor of all later forms, came into existence.
claims.quote: The whole history of the world, as at present known, although of a length quite incomprehensible by us, will hereafter be recognised as a mere fragment of time, compared with the ages which have elapsed since the first creature, the progenitor of innumerable extinct and living descendants, was created.
claims.scope: history of life on earth
measurable_quantities: age of the earliest evidence of life
age of the base of the Silurian/Cambrian fossil record
claims.candidate_data: Radiometric ages from the Geologic Time Scale, Precambrian fossil records (Paleobiology Database) and molecular-clock estimates (TimeTree).

claims.section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
claims.label: Every mental power was acquired by gradation
claims.claim: Each mental power and capacity must have been acquired gradually, so psychology will rest on this foundation, and light will be thrown on the origin of man and his history.
